questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 6.6 Decision trees and 6.7 Descriptive statistics
questions.question:
The directors of Foxglove Bakery must decide whether to open a kiosk or a cafe as the second outlet.

(a)

Using the table, calculate the mean, the median and the range of daily customers, and comment on how well the mean represents a typical month.

[5]

(b)

Estimate the probability of a high-demand month from the trial data. Then calculate the expected annual profit after interest of each option using the finance director's probability and using your estimate.

[5]

(c)

Evaluate which option Foxglove Bakery should choose. Justify your answer with reference to your decision tree and to the descriptive statistics.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The twelve monthly figures are 40, 45, 38, 42, 120, 130, 125, 44, 41, 118, 135 and 46, giving a total of 924 customers a day across the months. (M1)

Mean = 924/12 = 77 customers a day. (A1)

Ordered, the two middle values are 45 and 46, so the median = (45 + 46)/2 = 45.5 customers a day. (A1)

Range = 135 - 38 = 97 customers a day. (A1)

The mean is a poor summary of a typical month. It is 31.5 customers a day above the median, and no month was close to it: five months clustered near 42 and five near 125, with the remaining two between. The distribution is bimodal, not symmetrical, so the mean describes a month that never happened. (A1)

(b) High-demand months are those above 80 customers a day: months 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11, so five of twelve. The trial estimate of the probability of high demand is 5/12 = 0.417. (M1)(A1)

Using the finance director's 0.6: kiosk = 0.6 x 40,000 + 0.4 x 10,000 = EUR 28,000; cafe = 0.6 x 120,000 + 0.4 x (-60,000) = EUR 48,000. (M1)(A1)

Interest: kiosk loan 40,000 x 6% = EUR 2,400; cafe loan 120,000 x 6% = EUR 7,200. Net expected profit: kiosk EUR 25,600; cafe EUR 40,800. (A1)

Using the trial estimate of 5/12: kiosk = (5/12) x 40,000 + (7/12) x 10,000 = EUR 22,500; cafe = (5/12) x 120,000 + (7/12) x (-60,000) = EUR 15,000. After interest: kiosk EUR 20,100; cafe EUR 7,800. (A1)

The two probabilities therefore rank the options differently.

(c) Indicative evaluation. On the finance director's probability the decision is straightforward. The cafe's expected profit of EUR 40,800 is more than half as much again as the kiosk's EUR 25,600, and the upside, EUR 120,000 in a good year, is the kind of return that would justify the larger loan. A decision tree drawn on a 0.6 chance of high demand points clearly to the cafe.

The descriptive statistics undermine the probability the tree uses. The mean of 77 customers a day is not a typical month: it sits between two clusters, and the median of 45.5 is the better guide to what most months look like. Five of the twelve months were high-demand, so the empirical probability is 0.417, not 0.6. Rerun with 5/12, the ranking reverses: the kiosk earns EUR 20,100 against the cafe's EUR 7,800. The kiosk is also the more robust choice, because its worst case is a profit of EUR 10,000 while the cafe's is a loss of EUR 60,000, half the size of the whole investment.

The evaluation therefore turns on the probability, and the probability is the one thing the directors cannot observe. If the town's economy really does deliver high demand six years in ten, the cafe is right; if the trial stall is representative, the cafe destroys value in most years and the interest payment makes the bad case worse. The strongest answers note that a decision tree is only as good as its probabilities, that the trial was one stall in one year, and that opening the kiosk first keeps the option open. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the decision tree gives a clean answer on an input the case contradicts. With a 0.6 probability of high demand the cafe's expected profit, EUR 40,800 after interest, is well above the kiosk's EUR 25,600, and a student who draws the tree and computes the expected values will recommend the cafe. The arithmetic is not the trap; the probability is.

The lever is that descriptive statistics can invalidate the input to a decision tree. The twelve monthly observations are bimodal: five months near 42 customers a day and five near 125, with nothing in between. The mean of 77 therefore describes no real month, and the median of 45.5 is the honest summary. Counting the months above the 80-customer threshold gives a probability of 5/12 = 0.417, not 0.6. Substituting it reverses the ranking, and the loan interest widens the gap: the cafe falls to EUR 7,800 while the kiosk holds at EUR 20,100.

The second lever is the shape of the downside. The kiosk's worst case is a profit of EUR 10,000; the cafe's is a loss of EUR 60,000, half the size of the investment. A mean and an expected value treat these symmetrically, but a small bakery facing a EUR 60,000 loss does not. The range of 97 customers a day is the number that carries this: it says demand is not merely uncertain but bimodal, and bimodal demand is exactly where a single expected value is least trustworthy.

Classic wrong turns: using the mean of 77 as though it were typical; treating the 0.6 probability as data rather than an assumption; forgetting the interest; and comparing the cafe's upside with the kiosk's expected value instead of comparing like with like.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.2 The output of a flow line is set by its slowest stage, so adding capacity anywhere else produces nothing, and the choice between buying capacity at the bottleneck and buying overtime at the bottleneck is a choice between a fixed cost and a variable one
questions.question:
The manufacturer's four-stage line has one machine at each stage, and each machine is available for 2 400 minutes a week. The times per unit are given in the table. Demand is steady at 600 units a week and the manufacturer cannot meet it, so it is losing sales that it could otherwise make. The operations manager has two proposals. The first is to buy a second welding machine at a cost of 85 000 dollars, which would halve the time the welding stage takes per unit, and which would be depreciated over five years. The second is to work overtime at whichever stage is limiting output, at an overtime rate of 36 dollars an hour, which is available whenever it is needed and can be stopped at any time. The operations manager has also considered buying a second assembly machine and has asked what difference that would make, since assembly takes four minutes a unit and is the stage the manager believed to be the problem.

(a)

Calculate the weekly capacity of each of the four stages, and state which stage has the smallest capacity.

[3]

(b)

Determine the maximum number of units the line can produce in a week at present, and the shortfall against the weekly demand of 600 units.

[3]

(c)

Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second assembly machine, showing the capacity of every stage after the change.

[3]

(d)

Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second welding machine, and explain why the two answers in (c) and (d) differ.

[3]

(e)

Evaluate whether the manufacturer should buy the welding machine or pay for overtime, using the weekly costs of each and considering the manufacturer's circumstances.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The weekly capacity of a stage is the minutes available divided by the minutes each unit takes at that stage. With 2 400 minutes available at every stage:

Cutting: 2 400 / 3.0 = 800 units a week.
Welding: 2 400 / 5.0 = 480 units a week.
Assembly: 2 400 / 4.0 = 600 units a week.
Finishing: 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week.

The welding stage has the smallest capacity, at 480 units a week.

(b) A unit must pass through all four stages, so the line can produce no more units in a week than its slowest stage can pass. Welding is the slowest stage at 480 units a week, so the maximum weekly output is 480 units. Demand is 600 units a week, so the shortfall is 600 - 480 = 120 units a week, and those 120 units of sales are lost every week.

The other stages are not working at their limit. At an output of 480 units a week, cutting is using 480 x 3.0 = 1 440 of its 2 400 minutes, which is sixty per cent of its capacity; assembly is using 480 x 4.0 = 1 920 minutes, which is eighty per cent; and finishing is using 480 x 2.5 = 1 200 minutes, which is fifty per cent. Welding is using all 2 400 minutes, which is one hundred per cent.

(c) A second assembly machine halves the time assembly takes per unit, from 4.0 minutes to 2.0 minutes, so the capacity of assembly becomes 2 400 / 2.0 = 1 200 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 480 at welding, 1 200 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is still welding, at 480 units a week, so the output of the line does not change. It remains 480 units a week and the shortfall remains 120 units a week. The money spent on the second assembly machine buys no additional output at all, because assembly was not limiting the line; the 120 extra units a week that the second machine could pass through cannot reach it, since welding cannot send them on.

(d) A second welding machine halves the time welding takes per unit, from 5.0 minutes to 2.5 minutes, so the capacity of welding becomes 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 960 at welding, 600 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is now assembly, at 600 units a week, so the output of the line rises to 600 units a week, which is exactly the demand. The shortfall is closed. Welding is no longer the constraint and has spare capacity of 360 units a week; cutting is now the next tightest stage after assembly, at 800 units a week.

The two answers differ because output is governed by the slowest stage and by nothing else. In (c) the stage that was improved was not the slowest stage, so the line's output was still set by welding and did not move. In (d) the stage that was improved was the slowest stage, so the constraint moved to assembly and the output rose until it reached the new limit. Improving a stage that is not the constraint does not raise output; it only adds idle capacity to a stage that already had some. This is why the operations manager's belief that assembly was the problem was mistaken: assembly takes four minutes a unit, which is longer than cutting and longer than finishing, but welding takes five, and it is the longest time per unit that sets the pace.

(e) Either route closes the 120-unit shortfall, and the choice turns on the shape of the cost rather than on the size of it.

Overtime at the welding stage costs 36 dollars an hour. To make 120 extra units at 5.0 minutes a unit requires 120 x 5.0 = 600 minutes, which is 10 hours a week. At 36 dollars an hour that is 360 dollars a week, or 18 720 dollars a year. Overtime is a variable cost: it is paid only when the extra output is wanted, and it can be stopped in a week in which demand falls.

The welding machine costs 85 000 dollars depreciated over five years, which is 17 000 dollars a year, or about 326.92 dollars a week. It is a fixed cost: it is incurred every week whether the extra 120 units are made or not, and it commits the manufacturer for five years.

On cost alone the machine is slightly cheaper, at about 326.92 dollars a week against 360 dollars a week, which is about 2.72 dollars per extra unit against 3.00 dollars. Over five years the saving is roughly 1 720 dollars a year, about 8 600 dollars in total, which is small against an outlay of 85 000 dollars, and the payback on the machine is very long if it is justified only by the shortfall. The machine does have advantages beyond the weekly cost. It raises welding capacity to 960 units a week, so it leaves room for demand to grow to 600 units without any further spending, whereas overtime has to be paid for every extra unit and becomes more expensive if demand rises. It also removes the dependence on staff being willing to work overtime week after week, which is difficult to sustain and which raises the risk of absence and of poor quality on a tired shift.

Against that, the machine is a commitment. If demand falls, the 85 000 dollars is spent and the depreciation continues, while overtime can be cancelled. The manufacturer's position is not stated in the case, and the recommendation has to turn on it.

On the information given, the manufacturer should pay the overtime in the first instance, and revisit the machine if demand rises or proves to be permanent. The shortfall is 120 units a week, which is twenty per cent of demand, and the cost difference between the two routes is small enough, about 33 dollars a week, that it does not by itself justify an 85 000-dollar commitment. Overtime keeps the manufacturer flexible while it establishes whether the extra demand is durable, and it can be replaced by the machine once the demand has been shown to be permanent. The machine becomes the better choice as soon as demand is expected to rise towards the new welding capacity of 960 units, or as soon as the overtime proves difficult to staff; at that point the fixed cost is being spread over a larger output and the flexibility that overtime buys is no longer worth its price.
questions.explanation:
The theory of constraints is one of the few ideas in operations management that is both simple and counter-intuitive, and this item is arranged so that the counter-intuitive part cannot be avoided. The line has four stages, the times per unit are given, and the capacities follow by division. Nothing about the first two parts is hard. The third part then spends money on the stage the operations manager believes to be the problem, and the correct answer is that the spending achieves nothing.

That answer is available only to a candidate who has understood that output is set by the slowest stage. A candidate who has learned the calculation but not the idea will compute the new capacity of assembly, see that it has risen from 600 to 1 200 units a week, and report that output has risen. The item is designed so that this error produces a plausible, internally consistent and entirely wrong answer, which is why parts (c) and (d) are the same calculation applied to two stages and are marked separately. A candidate who gets (c) wrong will usually get (d) right, since improving the bottleneck obviously helps, and the pair together therefore separates understanding from procedure.

The last part moves from the physical constraint to the commercial one. Both routes close the shortfall, and the weekly costs are close: about 326.92 dollars for the machine against 360 dollars for the overtime. A candidate who decides on the weekly cost alone will choose the machine and will be able to justify it, but the justification is thin, because the difference is about 33 dollars a week against a commitment of 85 000 dollars. The interesting question is which cost is fixed and which is variable, and the case gives no information about how durable the demand is, so the honest answer is conditional: buy the flexibility first and the capacity later, unless the demand is known to be permanent. The item rewards that conditionality, and it rewards the candidate who notices that the machine also raises welding capacity beyond demand and therefore has value that the overtime route does not.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.4 / 3.8 / 6.3 Reshoring decision with landed cost and working capital effects
questions.question:
Using the case study and the cost data, answer all three parts.

(a)

Calculate the total landed cost per unit for the offshore option and for the domestic option, and calculate the increase in annual production cost if Vantar reshores.

[4]

(b)

Evaluate whether Vantar should move production to the domestic factory, taking into account the effect on stockholding and the markdowns described in the case study.

[6]

(c)

To what extent do factors other than cost determine the right decision for Vantar? Refer to at least two external factors in your answer.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Offshore: $\text{CIF}=14.00+1.20=\unicode{8364}15.20$; the tariff is $12\%$ of $\unicode{8364}15.20=\unicode{8364}1.82$; adding $\unicode{8364}0.30$ handling gives a landed cost of $\unicode{8364}17.32$ per unit. (M1)(A1) Domestic: $21.50+0.25=\unicode{8364}21.75$ per unit. (A1) The increase is $\unicode{8364}4.43$ per unit, so across $180\,000$ units the annual production cost rises by $4.426\times180\,000=\unicode{8364}796\,680$, about $\unicode{8364}797\,000$. (M1)(A1)

(b) On unit cost alone the move looks wrong: $\unicode{8364}4.43$ is a $25.5\%$ increase in the cost of every item. (A1) Two effects work against that conclusion. First, average stock falls from $\unicode{8364}2.10$ m to $\unicode{8364}0.72$ m, a release of $\unicode{8364}1.38$ m, and at an annual holding cost of $18\%$ that saves $1.38\times0.18=\unicode{8364}248\,400$ a year. (M1)(A1) Second, a nine-day lead time allows reorders during the season rather than a single pre-commitment, so the markdown problem largely disappears: $4\%$ of $180\,000$ units is $7\,200$ units, currently discounted by $35\%$ of $\unicode{8364}59$, which is about $\unicode{8364}148\,700$ of lost margin a year. (M1)(A1) Together these recover about $\unicode{8364}397\,000$, so the net additional cost is roughly $\unicode{8364}797\,000-\unicode{8364}397\,000=\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year, or $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit — about $3.8\%$ of the $\unicode{8364}59$ retail price, not the $25\%$ headline figure. (A1)

Against that residual cost must be set a shorter cash cycle, far less risk of being left with a season's worth of unwanted stock, and the marketing value of being able to promote a domestic supply chain. (A1) A balanced evaluation is that the move is financially defensible if Vantar can recover $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit through a modest price rise or through the higher full-price sell-through that reordering makes possible, and it is not defensible if the market will not bear any increase at all. The decisive question is therefore not cost but price elasticity, which the data do not give. (R1)

(c) To a considerable extent, because the cost gap after the stock and markdown effects is small enough that external factors can easily dominate it. (A1) *Political:* the offshore option depends on a $12\%$ tariff that a trade dispute could raise overnight; a five-point increase would add about $\unicode{8364}0.76$ to every unit and close a third of the remaining gap by itself, and this risk is entirely outside Vantar's control. (M1)(A1) *Environmental and ethical:* the company sells technical outdoor clothing to customers who are unusually attentive to provenance, and a domestic supply chain with a much shorter transport leg is a marketing asset that does not appear in the cost comparison at all; conversely, moving production offshore to a jurisdiction with weaker labour protections would carry reputational risk that could cost more than $\unicode{8364}400\,000$. (M1)(A1) *Economic:* a domestic factory removes exposure to freight-cost volatility and to currency movement on a $\unicode{8364}2.52$ m annual import bill. (A1) The counter-argument is that $\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year is real money and that none of these factors is certain, so the decision remains finely balanced; but where the quantified gap is under four per cent of retail price, factors that cannot be quantified will usually decide it. (R1)
questions.explanation: The item is built around a gap between the number a student computes first and the number that matters. The unit-cost comparison — €17.32 against €21.75 — is unambiguous and points one way, and a candidate who stops there concludes that reshoring is obviously wrong. The two effects that reverse the picture are both in the stimulus rather than in the cost table: €1.38m of stock is released, worth €248,400 a year at an 18% holding cost, and 53 days of lead time are removed, which is what allows the markdown problem to be solved at all. Neither appears in a unit cost, and that is the point — a landed-cost calculation systematically excludes working capital and obsolescence, both of which can exceed the cost difference it is being used to measure. Part (c) then asks the candidate to weigh factors that cannot be quantified against a residual gap of about €2.22 per unit, and the honest answer is that a gap of under four per cent of retail price is small enough that a tariff change or a reputational effect could overturn it. That is a genuinely transferable conclusion about offshoring decisions and is why the figures were calibrated to produce it. The item also rewards candidates who notice what the data do not contain. Nothing in the case study says how price-sensitive Vantar's customers are, and the entire recommendation rests on it: if the market will absorb €2.22 then the move is straightforward, and if it will not then the move destroys value. Naming the missing variable, and saying what it would take to find it out, is a stronger answer than any amount of further arithmetic on the figures already given.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.5 A contract that crosses the relevant range: the range of order sizes for which a positive contribution still destroys profit
questions.question:
The graph shows Kestrel's monthly profit plotted against the size of the contract. Answer every part with reference to the relevant range, and give money answers to the nearest pound and output answers to the nearest whole unit.

(a)

Calculate the contribution per unit at the current selling price, the monthly break-even output, and Kestrel's current monthly profit.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the contribution per unit on the contract, and Kestrel's monthly profit if a contract for 2 500 units per month is accepted.

[3]

(c)

Determine the range of contract sizes, if any, for which accepting the contract would leave Kestrel with a lower monthly profit than it earns now, and determine the smallest contract size at which crossing into the second shift becomes worthwhile.

[4]

(d)

The retailer's final offer is 2 500 units per month for one year. Evaluate the finance director's claim that the contract must be accepted because every unit adds to contribution, and recommend one change to the terms that would make the contract worth accepting.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Contribution per unit at the current price is £25 − £13 = £12 (A1). Break-even output is fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit, £48 000 ÷ £12 = 4 000 units per month (M1)(A1). Current output is exactly 4 000 units, so the current monthly profit is 4 000 × £12 − £48 000 = £0: the business is precisely at break-even.
(b) On the contract the price is £20, so the contribution per unit is £20 − £13 = £7 (A1). A contract of 2 500 units takes total output to 4 000 + 2 500 = 6 500 units, which is above the 6 000-unit ceiling of the first shift, so fixed costs rise to £48 000 + £18 000 = £66 000 (M1). Total contribution is 4 000 × £12 + 2 500 × £7 = £48 000 + £17 500 = £65 500, so the monthly profit becomes £65 500 − £66 000 = −£500 (A1). Kestrel would move from breaking even to losing £500 a month.
(c) Let q be the contract size. While 4 000 + q ≤ 6 000, that is q ≤ 2 000, no second shift is needed and profit is 7q, which is positive for every q > 0 (M1). Once q > 2 000 the extra £18 000 of fixed cost is incurred, so profit is 7q − 18 000, which is negative for q < 18 000 ÷ 7 = 2 571.43, that is up to and including 2 571 units (M1)(A1). The contract therefore leaves Kestrel worse off than it is now for every size from 2 001 to 2 571 units inclusive (A1), and the smallest size at which the step repays its own cost is 2 572 units, where profit is 7 × 2 572 − 18 000 = £4 (A1). Profit is not monotonic in the size of the contract: 2 000 units earns £14 000, 2 001 units loses £3 993, and 2 572 units earns £4.
(d) The director's claim is true of the unit and false of the decision. Each contract unit does add £7, but the relevant comparison is not between £7 and zero; it is between the £17 500 the contract contributes and the £18 000 of fixed cost that exists only because the contract was taken (M1). At 2 500 units the contract therefore reduces profit from £0 to −£500 a month, and because the contract runs for a year the loss is about −£6 000 over its life, before any allowance for the disruption of running a second shift for twelve months (A1). Two things qualify this. First, the arithmetic is knife-edge: a loss of £500 a month is 0.8% of monthly contribution, so a small change in the terms reverses the answer, and the business may rationally accept a marginal loss to secure a national listing (A1). Second, the loss is a property of the size and not of the idea: the contract is profitable below 2 001 units and above 2 571 units. The recommendation is to renegotiate one of the two (M1). At 2 500 units the contribution per unit must satisfy 2 500c ≥ 18 000, so c ≥ £7.20 and the price must be at least £20.20; alternatively the contract should be capped at 2 000 units or raised to at least 2 572 units (A1).
questions.explanation:
The item is built around a quantity that the syllabus names but that questions almost never test: the relevant range. Break-even analysis is linear inside one range and stops being linear at its edge, and the standard classroom treatment of a special order asks only whether the order's contribution is positive. Here it is, and the order is still wrong, because the order is also the cause of a step in fixed costs that no unit-level calculation can see.

The structure is chosen so that the obvious remedy and the correct remedy are different in kind. A candidate who reaches for contribution answers (b) as £17 500 and stops. The candidate has to discover the step, then discover that the step is caused by the decision rather than merely coincident with it, and then discover the shape of the result: profit is discontinuous at 2 000 units and *rises* again afterwards, so both 'small enough to stay on one shift' and 'large enough to pay for the second' are correct answers and the sizes between them are the only wrong ones. That is a genuinely different task from computing a break-even output, and it is the task a manager actually faces when a large customer's order arrives.

Part (d) is not decoration. Because the loss is £500 against £65 500 of contribution, the arithmetic alone does not settle the decision, and the candidate has to say so while still reaching a recommendation — which is why the mark scheme rewards a renegotiated figure rather than a bare accept or reject.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 4.4 Non-response that is not random: recovering the population figure from two segment readings instead of from the pooled sample
questions.question:
The chart compares the composition of the membership with the composition of the achieved sample. Use the data to answer the following.

(a)

Calculate the response rate for each segment and for the survey as a whole, and use them to show that the achieved sample is not representative of the membership.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the percentage of all respondents who said they would use the climbing wall, and state the conclusion the marketing manager draws from it.

[3]

(c)

Using the known size of each segment, determine a weighted estimate of the percentage of all 400 members who would use the wall, and hence estimate how many members that is. Explain why this figure differs from the one in part (b), and why the direction of the difference could have been predicted before any calculation.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate the marketing manager's claim that a majority of members want the climbing wall, and recommend how Northgate should have run or reported the survey so that the claim could be tested.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Premium response rate: 80 ÷ 100 = 80%. Standard response rate: 90 ÷ 300 = 30%. Overall: 170 ÷ 400 = 42.5% (M1)(A1). Premium members are a quarter of the membership, 100 ÷ 400 = 25%, but they are 80 of the 170 responses, which is 47.1% of the achieved sample (A1). A sample in which one segment is represented at nearly twice its true weight is not representative, and the cause is visible in the response rates: premium members were more than two and a half times as likely to reply.
(b) Of the 170 responses, 56 + 36 = 92 said they would use the wall, so the pooled figure is 92 ÷ 170 = 54.1% (M1)(A1). The manager concludes that a majority — more than half — of members want the climbing wall, and recommends approval (A1).
(c) Weight each segment's approval rate by its share of the membership. Premium approval is 56 ÷ 80 = 70% and standard approval is 36 ÷ 90 = 40%. The weighted estimate is 0.25 × 70% + 0.75 × 40% = 17.5% + 30% = 47.5% (M1)(A1), which is 0.475 × 400 = 190 of the 400 members (A1). The pooled figure is higher because the sample contains too many premium members, and premium members are the segment that wants the wall most: 70% against 40%, a gap of thirty percentage points. The direction of the error was predictable before any arithmetic, because the segment with the higher response rate is also the segment with the higher approval rate, so self-selection must inflate the pooled answer (A1).
(d) The claim is not supported. The weighted estimate is 47.5%, which is below half, and 190 of 400 members is 10 short of a majority (M1). Two things qualify this. First, 47.5% is itself an estimate resting on the assumption that non-respondents in each segment resemble respondents in that segment — an assumption the data cannot test, and one that is least safe here, since people who did not bother to answer a questionnaire about a climbing wall may be people who do not want a climbing wall (A1). Second, the commercial case may not need a majority: if premium members generate most of the revenue and 70% of them want the wall, the board might rationally build it anyway (A1). The recommendation is to re-run the survey so that the answer can be tested rather than assumed: weight the responses, or use quota sampling with a target of 100 premium and 300 standard members, follow up non-respondents, and report the result by segment with the response rate stated alongside it (M1)(A1).
questions.explanation:
The item attacks the most common error in the market research topic, which is not a calculation error at all. Students are taught that a bigger sample is a better sample, and a sample of 170 from a population of 400 looks excellent: it is 42.5% of every member. The error is invisible in the pooled figures and appears the moment the sample is split by segment.

The design makes the two errors point the same way on purpose. Non-response is only a bias if the people who do not answer differ from those who do, so the item gives the student the means to see that difference (80% against 30%) and a payoff for seeing it (70% against 40%). The population figure is then recoverable from two aggregate readings — the two segment approval rates — combined with the known segment sizes, and it falls on the other side of the majority line the manager claimed. Recovering a whole from weighted parts is the actual skill, and it is the one a manager needs when a survey comes back looking decisive.

Part (d) keeps the item honest. The weighted estimate is still an assumption about people who did not answer, so the correct conclusion is that the manager's claim is unproven rather than false — a distinction that matters more, in practice, than the arithmetic that precedes it.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 6.7 An open-ended final class: the mean is not estimable and the median is, and the target has to be judged on the second
questions.question:
The histogram shows the same distribution, with the open-ended final class drawn as a faded bar. Use the n/2 convention for the median and quartiles of a grouped distribution, and give all answers to two decimal places.

(a)

Reproduce the HR director's estimate of the mean from the grouped table, stating the assumption you have to make about the final class in order to produce it.

[3]

(b)

Determine the median and the interquartile range of the distribution, and state what assumption, if any, the open-ended class forces you to make in order to find them.

[3]

(c)

Show that no upper bound can be placed on the mean from this table, and determine the greatest lower bound that the table does guarantee.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate the HR director's claim that the mean absence is 5.71 days and that the six-day target has been met, and recommend how absence should be reported instead.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Using midpoints 1, 4, 7 and 10 for the first four classes and assuming the last class has the same width as the others, so a midpoint of 13 (M1), the estimated mean is (14 × 1 + 23 × 4 + 18 × 7 + 9 × 10 + 6 × 13) ÷ 70 = (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 78) ÷ 70 = 400 ÷ 70 = 5.71 days (A1). The assumption is that the six employees in the open class were each absent for about 13 days; nothing in the table supports it, and the class was left open precisely because those six records were not broken down (A1).
(b) With 70 employees the median is the 35th value. Cumulative frequencies are 14, 37, 55, 64 and 70, so the 35th value lies in the class 3 – 5, whose lower boundary is 2.5 and whose width is 3: median = 2.5 + ((35 − 14) ÷ 23) × 3 = 2.5 + 2.74 = 5.24 days (M1)(A1). The lower quartile is the 17.5th value, also in 3 – 5: 2.5 + ((17.5 − 14) ÷ 23) × 3 = 2.96 days. The upper quartile is the 52.5th value, in 6 – 8: 5.5 + ((52.5 − 37) ÷ 18) × 3 = 8.08 days. The interquartile range is 8.08 − 2.96 = 5.13 days (A1). No assumption is needed: these are positional measures, and the six employees in the open class affect them only by standing above them in the ordering.
(c) The six employees in the final class each have at least 12 days, but the table places no ceiling on them. If they each had 60 days, the mean would be (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 6 × 60) ÷ 70 = 682 ÷ 70 = 9.74 days (M1); if they each had 200 days it would be 21.74 days (A1). Since the assumed value can be increased without limit, no upper bound on the mean can be derived from the table (A1). The smallest the mean can be is when all six are at the foot of their class, 12 days: (14 + 92 + 126 + 90 + 72) ÷ 70 = 394 ÷ 70 = 5.63 days, so the table guarantees only that the mean is at least 5.63 days (A1).
(d) The claim is unsound in two ways. The figure of 5.71 days is not an estimate of the mean at all: it is the value obtained when the six longest absences are each assumed to be 13 days, and the same table is consistent with a mean of 9.74 days or of 21 days, so the mean cannot be compared with the target (M1)(A1). What the table does support is a different statement: the median is 5.24 days and therefore below the target, 8.6% of the workforce (6 of 70) were absent for at least 12 days, and the distribution is right-skewed with an interquartile range of 5.13 days — so the typical employee is comfortably inside the target and a small group is far outside it (A1). The recommendation is to report absence with positional measures and the tail: the median, the interquartile range and the percentage of employees above a threshold such as twelve days, together with the exact figures for the six long-term cases, which the HR department already holds (M1)(A1).
questions.explanation:
Every grouped-data question a student meets asks for an estimated mean, and the method — midpoint times frequency, summed and divided — becomes a reflex. This item is built so that the reflex produces a number that looks exactly like the right kind of answer and cannot be right, because one of the inputs does not exist.

The open-ended class is doing two jobs. Mechanically, it removes the midpoint, so the mean is not approximate but underivable, and the student has to say what the table still guarantees instead — a one-sided bound. Conceptually, it removes the *wrong* summary from the board's hands: the six employees who caused the class to be left open are the ones the business needs to manage, and the mean is the one statistic that lets them disappear into an average. The median and the interquartile range are unaffected by how large their values are, which is precisely why they are the right measures for a skewed distribution with a long tail.

The judgement in (d) is therefore not an add-on. A student who simply reports that the target is unmet has missed the more useful finding: the typical employee is well inside the target, 8.6% are far outside it, and those are different problems requiring different responses. Reporting the median does not conceal those six cases: it reports them as a percentage of the workforce rather than averaging them into a figure that no longer describes anybody, which is what the board's target actually needs.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.2 The stage with the lowest stated capacity is not the bottleneck: quantifying what the wrong investment buys
questions.question:
The diagram shows the three stages with their stated capacities. Answer every part, giving output to one decimal place and money to the nearest pound.

(a)

Determine the current maximum output of good units per hour and identify the stage that constrains it.

[3]

(b)

Explain why finishing, which has the lowest stated capacity of the three stages, is not the constraint.

[3]

(c)

Calculate the output of good units per hour under each proposal on its own and under both together, and calculate the cost per additional unit of hourly capacity in each case.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate which proposal, or pair of proposals, Trentvale should approve, using the payback period and two other factors.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Cutting can supply 100 units an hour but machining can process only 90, so the line is throttled to 90 units an hour at machining (M1). Of those, 10% are scrapped, so the good output is 90 × 0.90 = 81 units an hour (A1). Finishing can handle 84 units an hour and receives 81, so it is not full. The maximum output of good units is therefore 81 per hour and the constraint is machining (A1).
(b) A stage constrains the line only if the good units arriving at it exceed what it can process. Finishing receives 81 good units an hour and can process 84, so it runs with three units an hour, or 3.6%, of spare capacity (M1)(A1). Its stated capacity is the lowest of the three only because it is quoted before the scrap that happens upstream of it; comparing stated capacities compares the stages at different points in the process, and the comparison that matters is between good units delivered and capacity available at the same point (A1).
(c) Proposal 1 alone leaves machining untouched, so output stays at 81 units an hour: the extra finishing capacity is starved and the proposal adds nothing at all (M1). Proposal 2 alone raises good output from machining to 90 × 0.95 = 85.5 units an hour, but finishing can take only 84, so the line delivers 84 units an hour, a gain of 3 units an hour (A1). Both together deliver 85.5 units an hour, a gain of 4.5 units an hour (A1). Cost per additional unit of hourly capacity: Proposal 1, £250 000 for no additional units, so the cost per unit is undefined — no price buys the extra capacity at any level of spending; Proposal 2, £250 000 ÷ 3 = £83 333; both, £500 000 ÷ 4.5 = £111 111, of which the marginal £250 000 buys only 1.5 units an hour, or £166 667 each (A1).
(d) Proposal 2 is the one to approve. It adds 3 units an hour, which is 3 × 40 × 48 = 5 760 units a year and 5 760 × £18 = £103 680 of additional contribution, so it pays back in £250 000 ÷ £103 680 = 2.41 years (M1)(A1). Proposal 1 on its own pays back never: it adds no output, so there is no additional contribution against which to recover the £250 000, and it would add depreciation to a stage that already has spare capacity (A1). Two further considerations qualify the recommendation. First, scrap is not only lost output: every scrapped unit has already absorbed £22 of material and machining time, so reducing the scrap rate also improves material productivity and reduces waste disposal, benefits that the contribution calculation does not capture (A1). Second, doing both proposals raises output by a further 1.5 units an hour but costs another £250 000 and stretches payback to 3.21 years; that is worth doing only if Trentvale is confident of selling the extra 8 640 units a year, and demand, not capacity, may then become the constraint (A1).
questions.explanation:
Capacity questions invite one move: find the smallest number and call it the bottleneck. This item makes that move wrong in a way that is invisible in the data as presented, because the scrap rate is a property of one stage and its consequence lands on another. Finishing's 84 units an hour is measured in good units arriving; machining's 90 is measured in units started, of which a tenth never arrive. The two numbers are not comparable, and the whole item turns on converting them to a common basis.

The second design decision is to price the error rather than merely expose it. A question that asks only 'which stage is the bottleneck?' can be answered by luck; one that asks what £250 000 spent on the wrong stage buys forces the student to work out that it buys nothing at all — no output, no contribution, and therefore no payback period however long the horizon. That is a stronger and more practical idea than any definition of a bottleneck, and it is the reason the proposals cost the same: with equal price tags, the comparison is purely about what each one releases.

The sequencing result is the last turn. Proposal 1 is worthless alone and worth 1.5 units an hour once Proposal 2 is in place, so the value of a capital project here is not a property of the project but of the order in which it is done — which is exactly the situation the operations syllabus describes and the appraisal syllabus tends to ignore.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 3.8 Unequal asset lives, a replacement chain, and a common cost that cancels only in part
questions.question:
Vastra Teknik must choose between two machines for a four-year contract. The contract will
generate net cash inflows of $\pounds 90{,}000$ a year for each of the four years whichever machine
is used, so the choice turns entirely on the costs. The company's cost of capital is $10\%$ per
year and all cash flows arise at the ends of years.

Machine P costs $\pounds 120{,}000$ and has a working life of two years, so it must be replaced
by an identical machine at the end of year 2 at the same price. It is decommissioned at the end of
year 2 and again at the end of year 4.

Machine Q costs $\pounds 230{,}000$ and has a working life of four years, so it is not replaced.
It is decommissioned once, at the end of year 4.

The decommissioning charge is $\pounds D$ on each occasion it arises, and is the same for both
machines. Assume initially that $D = 20{,}000$.

(a) Calculate the payback period for each machine. \tag{3}

(b) Calculate the net present value of each machine over the four years, and state which machine
should be chosen on this basis. \tag{5}

(c) The finance director argues that the decommissioning charge can be ignored, because both
machines incur it and it will therefore cancel. Explain, with a calculation, why this is only
partly correct. \tag{4}

(d) Determine the value of $D$ at which the recommendation would change. \tag{4}

(a)

Calculate the payback period for each machine, taking no account for now of the replacement that machine P requires at the end of year 2.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the net present value of each machine over the four years, and state which machine should be chosen on this basis.

[5]

(c)

The finance director argues that the decommissioning charge can be ignored, because both machines incur it. Justify, with a calculation, why this is only partly correct.

[4]

(d)

Determine the value of $D$ at which the recommendation would change.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Machine P returns $\pounds 90{,}000$ a year against an outlay of $\pounds 120{,}000$, so

$$\text{payback}_{P} = \frac{120{,}000}{90{,}000} = 1.33 \text{ years}$$

which is about one year and four months (A1). Machine Q recovers $\pounds 230{,}000$ at the same
rate, so

$$\text{payback}_{Q} = \frac{230{,}000}{90{,}000} = 2.56 \text{ years}$$

or roughly two years and seven months (A1). On payback, P is the clear winner, recovering its cost
more than a year sooner (A1). Note that payback ignores the second purchase P must make at the end
of year 2, which is one reason the ranking it produces should not be trusted on its own.

(b) The four-year annuity factor at $10\%$ is

$$\frac{1}{1.1} + \frac{1}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{1}{1.1^{3}} + \frac{1}{1.1^{4}} = 3.1699$$

so the present value of the inflows, identical for both machines, is

$$90{,}000 \times 3.1699 = \pounds 285{,}288 \tag{A1}$$

For P the outflows are the purchase at $t = 0$, the replacement at $t = 2$, and decommissioning at
$t = 2$ and $t = 4$ (M1):

$$120{,}000 + \frac{120{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{4}}
= 120{,}000 + 99{,}174 + 16{,}529 + 13{,}660 = \pounds 249{,}363 \tag{A1}$$

For Q the outflows are the single purchase at $t = 0$ and decommissioning at $t = 4$ (M1):

$$230{,}000 + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{4}} = 230{,}000 + 13{,}660 = \pounds 243{,}660 \tag{A1}$$

Hence

$$\text{NPV}_{P} = 285{,}288 - 249{,}363 = \pounds 35{,}925, \qquad
\text{NPV}_{Q} = 285{,}288 - 243{,}660 = \pounds 41{,}628 \tag{A1}$$

Both are positive, so both are worth undertaking; on net present value Q should be chosen, by
$\pounds 5{,}702$ (A1). This reverses the payback ranking in (a), and it also reverses the average
rate of return, which favours P at $16.7\%$ against $12.0\%$ for Q precisely because P is measured
against a much smaller capital base.

(c) The director is right about one of the two payments and wrong about the other. Both machines
pay $D$ at the end of year 4, and that payment is multiplied by the same discount factor
$\frac{1}{1.1^{4}}$ in both columns, so it is common and does cancel (A1). Machine P, however, also
pays $D$ at the end of year 2, and Q pays nothing at that date; this payment has no counterpart to
cancel against (A1). Its present value is

$$\frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{2}} = \pounds 16{,}529 \tag{A1}$$

so the decommissioning charge contributes $\pounds 16{,}529$ to the difference between the two
machines — not zero, and not the $\pounds 33{,}058$ that a candidate who doubled it would report. The
claim is therefore only partly correct: the charge is irrelevant to the comparison in year 4 and
decisive in year 2 (A1).

The practical consequence is that the charge is not a detail. Without it the two machines would
differ by

$$(120{,}000 + 99{,}174) - 230{,}000 = -\pounds 10{,}826$$

in P's favour, and P would be chosen. It is the year-2 payment alone, worth $\pounds 16{,}529$, that
overturns a gap of $\pounds 10{,}826$ and turns the decision round.

(d) Let the decommissioning charge be $D$. The year-4 payments cancel as before, so the difference
between the present values of the two cost streams is

$$\left(120{,}000 + \frac{120{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{D}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{D}{1.1^{4}}\right)
- \left(230{,}000 + \frac{D}{1.1^{4}}\right) = -10{,}826 + \frac{D}{1.1^{2}} \tag{M1}$$

where the two $\frac{D}{1.1^{4}}$ terms have been cancelled (A1). Q is preferred while this is
positive and P while it is negative, so the recommendation changes where

$$-10{,}826 + \frac{D}{1.21} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D = 10{,}826 \times 1.21
= \pounds 13{,}100 \tag{A1}$$

At $D = 13{,}100$ the two machines are exactly equivalent, and the firm is indifferent (A1). Since
the actual charge of $\pounds 20{,}000$ exceeds $\pounds 13{,}100$, Q is confirmed as the better
choice — but the margin is $\pounds 5{,}702$, and a decommissioning quote that came in under
$\pounds 13{,}100$ would switch the decision to P.
questions.explanation:
This item turns on a piece of arithmetic that looks like bookkeeping and is in fact the
whole decision. Two identical charges are described in the same words, and the instinct is to treat
them the same way. They are not the same: one occurs at a date when both machines are spending money
and the other at a date when only one is. Discounting preserves that difference, nominal addition
destroys it, and the item is built so that the destroyed difference is larger than the gap it
overturns.

The naive path is to take the finance director at his word. If both decommissioning payments are
dropped, P costs $120{,}000 + 99{,}174 = \pounds 219{,}174$ against Q's $\pounds 230{,}000$, P wins
by $\pounds 10{,}826$, and no value of $D$ can change that — the answer to part (d) becomes 'the
charge makes no difference'. That is a confident, well-argued, entirely wrong answer, and it is
wrong because of one omission rather than one mistake. Nothing in the stem says the two payments
happen at different times; the candidate has to read the replacement chain and notice it.

What makes the item worth sixteen marks rather than six is that the correct treatment then has to be
carried through three different appraisal methods that disagree with each other. Payback favours P
by more than a year. Average rate of return favours P by nearly five percentage points, for the
reason that P is measured against a smaller capital base and is therefore flattered by any
percentage measure. Net present value favours Q, because it is the only one of the three that sees
the second purchase at the end of year 2 and the second decommissioning charge that comes with it.
A candidate who reports all three rankings and then recommends Q on the grounds that NPV accounts
for the timing of every cash flow over the full horizon has done the real work; a candidate who
reports one ranking and stops has not, however accurate the arithmetic.

The item is adapted from a UK A-Level investment-appraisal question that asks which of two machines
to buy given their purchase prices and running costs. The replacement chain, the decommissioning
charge, the partial cancellation and the break-even value of $D$ are all new here. The source asks
for a decision; this asks for the decision, for the term that produces it, and for the parameter
value at which it flips. That last move is what forces the cancellation to be understood rather than
performed, and it is why the item sits at difficulty 4 rather than 3.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.5 Break-even with a stepped fixed cost: two break-even points and a region of loss above the first
questions.question:
Kestrel Assembly makes a single product which it sells for $\pounds 14$. Variable cost is
$\pounds 6$ per unit.

Fixed costs are $\pounds 60{,}000$ a year for output up to and including $8{,}000$ units. Above
$8{,}000$ units a second shift is required, and fixed costs rise to $\pounds 85{,}000$ a year. The
step applies to the whole year's output, not only to the units above $8{,}000$, and there is no
change in selling price or variable cost.

(a) Calculate the break-even output on the assumption that fixed costs remain at
$\pounds 60{,}000$. \tag{3}

(b) Show that profit at an output of $8{,}000$ units is $\pounds 4{,}000$, while profit at an output
of $8{,}001$ units is $-\pounds 20{,}992$. \tag{5}

(c) Determine the output at which the business breaks even for the second time. \tag{4}

(d) Evaluate whether the business should plan an output of $10{,}000$ units, supporting your
answer with a calculation of the minimum selling price required. \tag{4}

(a)

Calculate the break-even output on the assumption that fixed costs remain at $60{,}000$.

[3]

(b)

Show that profit at an output of $8{,}000$ units is $4{,}000$, while profit at an output of $8{,}001$ units is $-20{,}992$.

[5]

(c)

Determine the output at which the business breaks even for the second time.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate whether the business should plan an output of $10{,}000$ units, supporting your answer with a calculation of the minimum selling price required.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Contribution per unit is

$$\pounds 14 - \pounds 6 = \pounds 8 \tag{A1}$$

and break-even output is fixed cost divided by contribution per unit (M1):

$$\frac{60{,}000}{8} = 7{,}500 \text{ units} \tag{A1}$$

This lies below $8{,}000$ units, so the $\pounds 60{,}000$ figure is the right one to use and the
answer is consistent.

(b) At $8{,}000$ units the higher fixed cost has not yet been triggered, so

$$\text{profit} = 8 \times 8{,}000 - 60{,}000 = 64{,}000 - 60{,}000 = \pounds 4{,}000 \tag{M1A1}$$

At $8{,}001$ units the step applies to the whole year's output, so fixed costs are
$\pounds 85{,}000$ and not $\pounds 60{,}000$ (M1):

$$\text{profit} = 8 \times 8{,}001 - 85{,}000 = 64{,}008 - 85{,}000 = -\pounds 20{,}992 \tag{A1}$$

The two figures differ by $\pounds 24{,}992$ even though output has risen by a single unit (A1). Of
that, $\pounds 8$ is the contribution earned by the extra unit and $\pounds 25{,}000$ is the step in
fixed cost, so almost the entire movement is the step and not the unit. A profit-and-loss account
drawn up for any output from $8{,}001$ units upwards must therefore use $\pounds 85{,}000$, and the
$7{,}500$-unit figure from (a) tells the business nothing about that region.

(c) In the upper band, fixed costs are $\pounds 85{,}000$ and contribution per unit is unchanged at
$\pounds 8$ (M1):

$$\frac{85{,}000}{8} = 10{,}625 \text{ units} \tag{A1}$$

At $10{,}625$ units contribution is $8 \times 10{,}625 = \pounds 85{,}000$, which exactly covers the
higher fixed cost, so profit is zero (A1). Because $10{,}625 > 8{,}000$ the answer lies inside the
band to which it applies and is self-consistent, exactly as in (a) (A1).

The business therefore breaks even twice, at $7{,}500$ units and again at $10{,}625$ units, and
makes a loss at every output in between, with the single worst point being $8{,}001$ units. Any
output from $10{,}626$ units upward is profitable. The margin of safety at a planned output of
$12{,}000$ units is $12{,}000 - 10{,}625 = 1{,}375$ units, or $11.5\%$ — measured against the second
break-even point, not the first, which would give a meaningless $37.5\%$.

(d) At $10{,}000$ units the business is in the upper band, so fixed costs are $\pounds 85{,}000$
(M1). Let the selling price be $p$; contribution per unit is $p - 6$ (M1). Break-even requires

$$10{,}000(p - 6) = 85{,}000 \tag{A1}$$

so

$$p = \frac{85{,}000}{10{,}000} + 6 = 8.50 + 6 = \pounds 14.50 \tag{A1}$$

The current price of $\pounds 14.00$ gives a contribution of $\pounds 80{,}000$ against fixed costs
of $\pounds 85{,}000$ and a loss of $\pounds 5{,}000$, so the required increase is $\pounds 0.50$,
or $3.6\%$. Two cautions are worth recording. The answer is the break-even price at this output, not
a recommended price: at $\pounds 14.50$ the business makes exactly nothing on $10{,}000$ units, and a
price below $\pounds 14.50$ loses money. And the answer is specific to $10{,}000$ units, because the
$\pounds 85{,}000$ is spread over whatever volume is actually produced; at $12{,}000$ units the
break-even price would be only $\pounds 13.08$.
questions.explanation:
Break-even analysis is one of the first quantitative tools a business student meets, and
it is normally taught as the answer to a single question: how many units must we sell? The formula
is short enough to memorise, and the memorised version carries an assumption that is almost never
examined — that the fixed cost stays fixed across the range of output being considered. Here it does
not, and the item is built so that the assumption fails exactly where a manager would most want to
rely on it.

The naive path is to compute contribution, divide, and stop: $60{,}000$ over $8$ gives $7{,}500$
units, the business plans to sell well above that, and everything looks sound. That answer is not
wrong as far as it goes, and it is self-consistent, which is what makes it dangerous. It says
nothing at all about the region above $8{,}000$ units, and in that region the same formula applied to
the same cost structure gives a loss of nearly $\pounds 21{,}000$. A manager acting on the first
number would expand output into the step and be worse off than before expanding, having been told by
the arithmetic that the expansion was safe.

The discontinuity is worth dwelling on, because it is the point that separates understanding the
formula from being able to use it. Profit at $8{,}000$ units is $\pounds 4{,}000$; at $8{,}001$ it is
$-\pounds 20{,}992$. One extra unit destroys nearly $\pounds 25{,}000$ of profit, of which
$\pounds 8$ comes from the unit and the remaining $\pounds 25{,}000$ from the step. A candidate who
writes that down has understood that the step applies to the year's whole output rather than to the
marginal units, which is the single idea the item exists to test, and which the phrase "applies to
the whole year's output" in the stem is there to make decidable rather than ambiguous.

Two further moves carry the item past routine application. Part (c) asks for the second break-even
point and requires the candidate to check that the answer lies inside the band to which it applies
— the same consistency check that part (a) demanded, but now on the far side of the step, where the
obvious answer and the correct answer are different numbers. Part (d) then inverts the question,
fixing output and solving for price, which is the version a manager actually faces and which exposes
anyone who has been applying the formula mechanically: using $\pounds 60{,}000$ instead of
$\pounds 85{,}000$ here gives $\pounds 12.00$ and understates the required price by two pounds.

The item is adapted from a UK A-Level treatment of break-even that introduces a stepped fixed cost
and asks for the revised chart. Asking for the two break-even points explicitly, demanding the
profit figures on either side of the step so that the discontinuity has to be stated as a number,
and inverting to solve for price rather than for output are all new here. The source wants a
picture; this wants the candidate to locate a region of loss that a correctly drawn chart would show
but a single calculated figure would hide.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 2.1 Labour turnover as a weighted aggregate: recovering a missing department and targeting the right one
questions.question:
Haldane Logistics employs $250$ staff in three departments. The workforce plan records
the number of staff who left during the year, but the entry for department B has been lost.

| Department | Number employed | Number leaving during the year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 120 | 9 |
| B | 80 | not recorded |
| C | 50 | 11 |

The company's overall labour turnover for the year is known to have been $14.4\%$. Each leaver
costs the business $\pounds 3{,}500$ to replace, covering recruitment, training and lost output.

Labour turnover is calculated as

$$\text{labour turnover} = \frac{\text{number of staff leaving during the year}}
{\text{number of staff employed}} \times 100.$$

(a) Calculate the number of staff who left department B during the year. \tag{3}

(b) Calculate the labour turnover rate for each department and confirm the overall rate of
$14.4\%$. \tag{5}

(c) Show that the overall rate is not the average of the three departmental rates, and explain why
the difference arises. \tag{4}

(d) The human resources director proposes an overall target of $10\%$ and must choose between two
interventions: reducing department A's turnover to $5\%$, or reducing department C's turnover to
$10\%$. Evaluate which should be prioritised. \tag{4}

(a)

Calculate the number of staff who left department B during the year.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the labour turnover rate for each department and confirm the overall rate of $14.4$ per cent.

[5]

(c)

Show that the overall rate is not the average of the three departmental rates, and explain why the difference arises.

[4]

(d)

The human resources director proposes an overall target of $10$ per cent and must choose between reducing department A turnover to $5$ per cent and reducing department C turnover to $10$ per cent. Evaluate which should be prioritised.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Overall turnover of $14.4\%$ on $250$ staff gives a total of

$$0.144 \times 250 = 36 \text{ leavers} \tag{M1}$$

of which $9$ came from A and $11$ from C, so department B accounts for (M1)

$$36 - 9 - 11 = 16 \text{ leavers} \tag{A1}$$

(b) Applying the formula to each department in turn (M1):

$$\text{A}: \frac{9}{120} \times 100 = 7.5\%, \qquad
\text{B}: \frac{16}{80} \times 100 = 20.0\%, \qquad
\text{C}: \frac{11}{50} \times 100 = 22.0\% \tag{A1A1A1}$$

The overall rate is the total leaving divided by the total employed, not the average of the three
percentages:

$$\frac{9 + 16 + 11}{120 + 80 + 50} \times 100 = \frac{36}{250} \times 100 = 14.4\% \tag{M1A1}$$

which confirms the figure given.

(c) The simple average of the three departmental rates is

$$\frac{7.5 + 20.0 + 22.0}{3} = \frac{49.5}{3} = 16.5\% \tag{M1A1}$$

against a true overall rate of $14.4\%$, so the average overstates turnover by $2.1$ percentage
points (A1). The reason is that the departments are not the same size. The average gives each
department's rate a weight of one third, but department A actually employs $48\%$ of the workforce
and department C only $20\%$ (A1). The overall rate is a weighted mean in which each department's
rate is weighted by its headcount:

$$\frac{120(7.5) + 80(20.0) + 50(22.0)}{250}
= \frac{900 + 1{,}600 + 1{,}100}{250} = \frac{3{,}600}{250} = 14.4\%$$

The $7.5\%$ earned by the largest department pulls the figure down more than the $22\%$ earned by
the smallest pulls it up, which is exactly the effect the unweighted average discards.

(d) Reducing department A to $5\%$ means $0.05 \times 120 = 6$ leavers, a saving of $3$ (M1). Total
leavers fall to $33$ and the overall rate becomes

$$\frac{33}{250} \times 100 = 13.2\% \tag{A1}$$

an improvement of $1.2$ percentage points, at a saving of $3 \times 3{,}500 = \pounds 10{,}500$.

Reducing department C to $10\%$ means $0.10 \times 50 = 5$ leavers, a saving of $6$ (M1). Total
leavers fall to $30$ and the overall rate becomes

$$\frac{30}{250} \times 100 = 12.0\% \tag{A1}$$

an improvement of $2.4$ percentage points, at a saving of $6 \times 3{,}500 = \pounds 21{,}000$.

Department C should be prioritised. It delivers twice the reduction in the overall rate and twice
the cost saving, from $20\%$ of the workforce rather than $48\%$ (A1). The reason is that the
improvement depends on two things multiplied together — the size of the department and the size of
the cut — and department C's cut is $12$ percentage points against department A's $2.5$.

Two qualifications belong in a full answer. Neither intervention reaches the $10\%$ target on its
own: both together give $12.0\%$, and hitting $10\%$ would require $25$ leavers in total, so a
further five must come from somewhere. And the arithmetic is silent on why people leave. Department
C's $22\%$ may reflect working conditions, pay or management, and if the underlying cause is not
addressed the reduction may prove temporary; conversely, if department A's low turnover reflects a
genuinely well-managed operation, cutting it further may be the cheapest of all. The numbers say
where the leverage is, not what to do about it (A1).
questions.explanation:
Labour turnover is a ratio, and ratios built from parts do not behave like the parts.
Every student knows this in principle and almost nobody applies it under pressure, because the
unweighted average is quicker to compute and feels like a fair summary. This item makes the shortcut
cost something: the average gives $16.5\%$ against a true $14.4\%$, and a manager working from the
higher figure would set targets against a rate the business never had.

The naive path in part (d) is to read the three rates, see that department C is worst at $22\%$, and
then notice that department A is four times its size and conclude that A must be where the numbers
are. That is a plausible argument and it is wrong, because the gain from an intervention is the
product of two quantities rather than either one alone. Department A offers a cut of $2.5$
percentage points on $120$ staff, worth three leavers. Department C offers a cut of $12$ points on
$50$ staff, worth six. The smaller department wins by a factor of two, and it wins on cost as well
as on the headline rate, because the replacement cost attaches to leavers rather than to
percentages.

Part (a) is doing more work than it appears to. Recovering a missing component of an aggregate is
not a routine operation in a business context, and it forces the candidate to hold the aggregate and
its parts in mind at the same time — which is precisely the mental posture the rest of the item
needs. It also makes the weighted structure unavoidable in part (b), because the three departmental
rates have to reconcile with a total that was supplied before any of them was known.

The final part asks for an evaluation rather than a calculation, which is deliberate. The arithmetic
points one way and it points clearly, but it rests on an assumption — that turnover can be reduced by
a stated number of points in a chosen department — that the data does nothing to support. A candidate
who recommends C, gives the figures, and then observes that the cause of C's turnover is unknown and
that neither intervention reaches the target has done the whole question. One who produces only
$12.0\%$ and $13.2\%$ has done the arithmetic and stopped, and that is the difference between a
business answer and a numeracy answer.

The item is adapted from a UK A-Level human-resource data-response that supplies a table of
departmental turnover and asks which department the business should be most concerned about. Making
one entry missing so that the aggregate has to be recovered, making the smallest department the
highest-turnover one so that the rates and the contributions point in opposite directions, and
requiring the two interventions to be compared in both percentage and money terms are all new here.
The source asks for an identification; this asks for a decision that the identification would get
wrong.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 3.5 Two transactions that move the liquidity ratios in opposite directions, and the cancellation inside the acid test
questions.command_term: Calculate, Calculate, Calculate, Show that, Evaluate
questions.question:
Marlowe Supplies is a single-product wholesaler. The figures above are taken from its final accounts for the year just ended. Before those figures are finalised the business is considering two transactions: paying a supplier $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash, and then buying $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit.

(a)

Calculate the gross profit margin, the operating profit margin and the net profit margin.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the return on capital employed, stating which figure you have used as the numerator and which as the denominator.

[3]

(c)

Calculate the current ratio and the acid test ratio at the position shown.

[3]

(d)

The business pays a supplier $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash. Show that both the current ratio and the acid test ratio rise, and explain why a payment that reduces current assets and current liabilities by the same amount improves both ratios.

[3]

(e)

The business then buys $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit. Show that the acid test ratio falls to 0.81, and evaluate whether the two transactions together leave Marlowe Supplies in a stronger or a weaker liquidity position than it began in.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Gross profit is revenue less cost of goods sold, so (M1)

$$\pounds 480{,}000 - \pounds 300{,}000 = \pounds 180{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{180{,}000}{480{,}000} = 37.5\% \tag{A1}$$

Operating profit deducts the operating expenses: $\pounds 180{,}000 - \pounds 120{,}000 = \pounds 60{,}000$, so the operating profit margin is $60{,}000/480{,}000 = 12.5\%$ (A1).

Net profit also deducts interest and tax: $\pounds 60{,}000 - \pounds 12{,}000 - \pounds 9{,}600 = \pounds 38{,}400$, so the net profit margin is $38{,}400/480{,}000 = 8.0\%$ (A1).

The three margins fall by design: each one deducts a further layer of cost, so the sequence $37.5\%$, $12.5\%$, $8.0\%$ is a description of where the revenue goes. The largest single deduction is the $\pounds 120{,}000$ of operating expenses, which takes 25 percentage points of revenue and is the reason the gross margin is three times the operating margin.

(b) Capital employed is the long-term money in the business, which here is equity plus non-current liabilities (M1):

$$\pounds 200{,}000 + \pounds 100{,}000 = \pounds 300{,}000$$

Return on capital employed is operating profit divided by capital employed (M1):

$$\frac{60{,}000}{300{,}000} = 20.0\% \tag{A1}$$

The numerator must be operating profit, not net profit. Using net profit would give $38{,}400/300{,}000 = 12.8\%$, which understates the return on the assets because it charges the capital employed with interest that has already been deducted in arriving at net profit. Using equity alone as the denominator would give $60{,}000/200{,}000 = 30.0\%$, which overstates it by leaving the non-current liabilities out of the capital they helped to fund.

(c) Current assets are inventory, receivables and cash (M1):

$$\pounds 45{,}000 + \pounds 60{,}000 + \pounds 15{,}000 = \pounds 120{,}000$$

The current ratio is current assets over current liabilities (A1):

$$\frac{120{,}000}{60{,}000} = 2.00$$

The acid test removes inventory from the numerator, because inventory is the current asset least likely to convert to cash at its book value (A1):

$$\frac{120{,}000 - 45{,}000}{60{,}000} = \frac{75{,}000}{60{,}000} = 1.25$$

(d) Paying $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash reduces cash to $\pounds 5{,}000$, so current assets become $\pounds 110{,}000$ and current liabilities become $\pounds 50{,}000$ (M1).

$$\text{current ratio} = \frac{110{,}000}{50{,}000} = 2.20 \qquad \text{acid test} = \frac{110{,}000 - 45{,}000}{50{,}000} = \frac{65{,}000}{50{,}000} = 1.30 \tag{A1}$$

Both ratios rise, from 2.00 to 2.20 and from 1.25 to 1.30, even though the business is now smaller by $\pounds 10{,}000$ of cash (A1).

The reason is that the same amount leaves the top and the bottom of the fraction. Writing the current ratio as $a/b$ with $a > b$, the new ratio is $(a-x)/(b-x)$, and

$$\frac{a-x}{b-x} > \frac{a}{b} \iff b(a-x) > a(b-x) \iff ab - bx > ab - ax \iff a > b$$

so the ratio rises whenever the transaction removes equal amounts from both and the ratio was above one. The size of the payment does not matter, and neither does the fact that it is a payment: any transaction that reduces current assets and current liabilities by the same amount has this effect. The same algebra run in reverse shows that adding equal amounts to both *lowers* a ratio above one, which is what part (e) does.

(e) Buying $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit raises inventory to $\pounds 75{,}000$ and current liabilities to $\pounds 80{,}000$, so current assets become $\pounds 140{,}000$ (M1).

$$\text{current ratio} = \frac{140{,}000}{80{,}000} = 1.75 \tag{A1}$$

The acid test numerator is unchanged, because the $\pounds 30{,}000$ added to inventory is subtracted again (M1):

$$\frac{140{,}000 - 75{,}000}{80{,}000} = \frac{65{,}000}{80{,}000} = 0.8125 \approx 0.81 \tag{A1}$$

The two transactions together have moved the current ratio from 2.00 to 1.75 and the acid test from 1.25 to 0.81, so on balance the liquidity position is weaker, not stronger (A1).

The acid test is the ratio that should be read here, and the current ratio is the one that flatters. At 1.75 the current ratio still looks comfortable, and it has fallen by less than the acid test because inventory is doing the work: inventory is now $\pounds 75{,}000$ of $\pounds 140{,}000$ of current assets, so more than half of what the business counts as liquid is stock that has to be sold before it becomes cash. The acid test has crossed below 1.00, which means the business cannot settle its current liabilities from the assets it already holds in near-cash form. It would have to sell inventory, and selling inventory is what generates the receivables and cash in the first place, so the position is circular rather than merely tight.

The evaluation is not one-sided, however. The $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory was bought to be sold, and if it turns over as the existing stock does it will convert into receivables and then cash within the working capital cycle, restoring the acid test without any new financing. The $\pounds 10{,}000$ paid to the supplier also released credit and may have earned a settlement discount. So the transactions weaken the *reported* liquidity position while leaving the *underlying* trading position intact, and the honest conclusion is that the ratios have moved in a way the business should monitor rather than a way that shows it is in difficulty. What the figures cannot settle is how quickly the new inventory will turn over, and that is the question a lender would ask next.
questions.explanation:
Ratio analysis is taught as a set of formulas and marked as a set of answers, and the formulas are reliable enough that a student can score well on them without ever forming an opinion about what a ratio is. This item is aimed at the gap between using a ratio and reasoning with one. Parts (a) to (c) are the routine application, and they are included so that the item has a floor: a student who can do the arithmetic has something to show for the work. Parts (d) and (e) ask a different kind of question, and they cannot be answered by substituting into a formula at all.

The transaction in part (d) is counter-intuitive in a way that catches almost everyone the first time. A business pays its debts and its liquidity ratios improve; a business that pays its debts is poorer in cash and its ratios improve. Both statements are true, and the reason is that a ratio is a comparison rather than a measurement, so changing the numbers on both sides of it changes the comparison itself. The condition that decides the direction is whether the ratio was above one, and it is a property of the ratio and not of the transaction. Once a student has seen the algebra, the result stops being paradoxical, and the size of the payment stops mattering at all -- a theme the item makes explicit, because the instinct is to explain the movement by saying that ten thousand pounds is small.

Part (e) then turns the same machinery through ninety degrees. Buying inventory on credit adds equal amounts to current assets and current liabilities, so the equal-amounts rule applies and the current ratio falls. The acid test is the interesting case, because it subtracts inventory from the numerator, and the addition and the subtraction cancel exactly: the numerator is untouched while the denominator rises, so the ratio must fall and it falls below one. A student who has only memorised the equal-amounts rule will get the current ratio right and the acid test wrong, and the two answers will disagree with each other in a way that is visible on the page.

The final evaluation is deliberately open. The ratios have weakened and the conclusion that the position is weaker is defensible; so is the conclusion that the position is unchanged, because the inventory was bought to be sold and the acid test will recover as it turns over. What the item will not accept is a conclusion that ignores the reason the inventory is there. This is the standard AO3 demand in Business Management -- use the figures to reach a judgement, and recognise the limit of what the figures can show -- and it is the part of the subject that a purely computational preparation leaves out.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.5 A break-even output above the capacity ceiling: a negative margin of safety and the three single levers that would close the gap
questions.command_term: Calculate, Determine, Show that, Determine, Evaluate
questions.question:
Ridgeway Ceramics makes a single product on one kiln line. The selling price is $\pounds 40$ per unit and the variable cost is $\pounds 24$ per unit. Annual fixed costs are $\pounds 200{,}000$. The kiln line can produce at most $10{,}000$ units in a year, and there is no way to add a second line within the year.

(a)

Calculate the contribution per unit and the break-even output.

[3]

(b)

Determine the margin of safety in units and as a percentage of capacity, and explain what a negative margin of safety means for this business.

[3]

(c)

Show that the best result Ridgeway Ceramics can achieve in a year is a loss of $\pounds 40{,}000$.

[3]

(d)

Determine the value of the selling price at which the business would exactly break even at its current capacity, and state the corresponding value for the annual fixed costs and for the variable cost per unit, taking each of the three on its own.

[3]

(e)

Evaluate which of the three changes in part (d) the management of Ridgeway Ceramics is most likely to be able to make, and justify your answer.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Contribution per unit is the selling price less the variable cost per unit (M1):

$$\pounds 40 - \pounds 24 = \pounds 16 \tag{A1}$$

Break-even output is fixed costs divided by contribution per unit (A1):

$$\frac{200{,}000}{16} = 12{,}500 \text{ units}$$

(b) The margin of safety is the amount by which the planned output exceeds the break-even output, so with output at the capacity ceiling (M1):

$$10{,}000 - 12{,}500 = -2{,}500 \text{ units}$$

As a percentage of capacity (A1):

$$\frac{-2{,}500}{10{,}000} \times 100 = -25\%$$

A negative margin of safety means the business cannot reach break-even at any output it is able to produce (A1). Every unit it makes sells for $\pounds 16$ more than its variable cost, and that contribution is never enough to cover $\pounds 200{,}000$ of fixed costs, so the business makes a loss in every year in which it operates. The negative figure is not a shortfall to be made up by selling harder; it is a statement that the break-even point lies outside the set of outputs the business can reach.

(c) At full capacity the total contribution is (M1)

$$10{,}000 \times \pounds 16 = \pounds 160{,}000$$

and the loss is the fixed costs less that contribution (A1):

$$\pounds 160{,}000 - \pounds 200{,}000 = -\pounds 40{,}000$$

Because contribution per unit is positive, each additional unit sold reduces the loss by $\pounds 16$, so profit increases with output throughout the feasible range (M1). The largest output the line can produce is therefore the least unprofitable one, and $\pounds 40{,}000$ is a loss at the best point rather than at a poor one: there is no output at which Ridgeway Ceramics makes a profit, so the maximum profit it can achieve in a year is a loss of $\pounds 40{,}000$.

(d) Each change is found by setting the total contribution at capacity equal to the fixed costs.

For the selling price, let it be $p$ (M1):

$$10{,}000(p - 24) = 200{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p - 24 = 20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = \pounds 44.00 \tag{A1}$$

For the annual fixed costs, with contribution per unit still $\pounds 16$:

$$10{,}000 \times 16 = \pounds 160{,}000 \tag{A1}$$

For the variable cost per unit, let it be $v$:
