$$10{,}000(40 - v) = 200{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 40 - v = 20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \pounds 20.00 \tag{A1}$$

So the three thresholds are a price of $\pounds 44.00$ (a rise of $\pounds 4.00$, or 10%), fixed costs of $\pounds 160{,}000$ (a cut of $\pounds 40{,}000$, or 20%) and a variable cost of $\pounds 20.00$ (a cut of $\pounds 4.00$, or 16.7%). Each figure is a threshold and not a target: at exactly that value the business breaks even at full capacity and makes nothing, so any of the three has to be bettered before a profit appears.

(e) The three changes are not equally available, and the comparison has to be made on two axes: how large the change is, and whether the business controls it.

The price rise is the smallest proportional change and it requires no investment, no renegotiation and no new equipment, which makes it attractive on paper. It is also the least likely to hold. Ridgeway sells a single product into a market it does not control, and a 10% rise has to be accepted by every customer for the arithmetic to work; if it is accepted by fewer, the contribution gain on the remaining units does not compensate for the volume lost, and at a price of $\pounds 44$ the business needs *all* 10 000 units to break even, leaving no room for any loss of demand at all. The remedy that looks cleanest is the one with the narrowest margin for error.

The fixed-cost cut is the largest change in absolute terms, $\pounds 40{,}000$, and it is the one the business controls most directly, since fixed costs are largely internal commitments. But the kiln line is the fixed cost that matters, and it cannot be halved; a 20% reduction in a single-line ceramics business means cutting maintenance, staffing or the second shift, and cutting the second shift is precisely what would reduce capacity and make the position worse. A fixed-cost cut that lowers the ceiling lowers the output the business can sell, and the break-even output would have to be recalculated against the smaller capacity rather than assumed unchanged.

The variable-cost cut is the one most likely to be achievable. $\pounds 4.00$ per unit is a 16.7% reduction in the cost of materials and power, and variable costs are the category a manufacturer can most often attack: renegotiating a clay or glaze contract, reducing kiln waste, buying in larger quantities. It requires no change to the price the customer sees and no reduction in capacity, so it does not trade one problem for another. The difficulty is that a 16.7% cut is substantial for a business whose inputs are commodity-like, and any saving is likely to arrive in stages rather than at once.

Taken together, the most likely single change is the variable-cost reduction, and the strongest reason is not that it is the largest or the smallest but that it is the only one that leaves the capacity ceiling and the selling price untouched. The most reliable answer, however, is not to rely on any single lever: a smaller price rise combined with a smaller variable-cost reduction reaches the same threshold while exposing the business to less risk on either one, and a management that pursues only one of the three is betting the whole recovery on the assumption that is hardest to verify. What the figures cannot show is how the market would respond to a price rise or how far a supplier would move, and those are the questions that decide between the options.
questions.explanation:
Break-even is the first quantitative tool a business student meets, and it is almost always presented as a question with an answer: how many units must we sell? The formula is short, the answer is a number, and the number is treated as reachable. This item is built on the observation that the formula contains no capacity, so it will happily produce an answer the business cannot act on. Nothing in the calculation is wrong; what is wrong is the assumption, imported from every exercise the student has seen, that the break-even output is within the range of outputs the business can produce.

That assumption is normally harmless, which is what makes it worth attacking. In a well-posed question the break-even point sits below capacity, the margin of safety is positive, and the tool behaves as advertised. Here it sits 2 500 units above capacity, and every conclusion drawn from the standard reading of the result inverts: the business cannot become profitable by selling more, because selling more is already the best it can do and it still loses money. The margin of safety, which students are taught to read as a cushion, becomes a measure of how far outside the achievable range the break-even point lies.

The item also rewards a student who understands what contribution per unit does and does not mean. A positive contribution means each unit reduces the loss, so the loss is smallest at the largest feasible output. A student who has memorised "profit rises with output above break-even" will look for the profitable region and find none, and the honest conclusion -- that the best available outcome is a loss -- is the one the item is testing for. That conclusion is uncomfortable, and reaching it requires the student to report a result that no textbook exercise would ask for.

The final part moves the item from analysis to judgement, which is where the Business Management assessment objectives live. Three thresholds have been calculated and they are arithmetically interchangeable; deciding between them requires knowledge of the business that the numbers do not contain. The item does not have a single right answer, and it is marked as though it does not: what is assessed is whether the student can say why one lever is more available than another, and whether they notice that a fixed-cost cut in a single-line manufacturer may take capacity down with it. That last observation is the one that separates a student who has understood the model from one who has only learned to use it.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 4.5 A revenue-positive, profit-negative price cut: price elasticity of demand governs turnover, but contribution per member governs profit once a variable cost sits under the price
questions.command_term: Calculate, Calculate, Show that, Determine, Evaluate
questions.question:
The manager of Highfield Fitness wants to fill the gym by cutting the monthly fee, and argues that the extra memberships will raise revenue. Using the figures in the stimulus, calculate the present revenue, contribution and profit; calculate the price elasticity of demand implied by the proposal; show what the cut would do to revenue and to profit; determine the membership the gym would actually need to hold profit where it is; and evaluate whether the cut should be made.

(a)

Calculate the gym's current monthly revenue, its contribution per member, its total monthly contribution and its monthly profit.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the price elasticity of demand implied by the manager's figures, and state whether demand is price-elastic or price-inelastic over this price range.

[3]

(c)

Show that the price cut raises monthly revenue to $£12{,}240$ but reduces monthly profit to $£2{,}080$, and comment on why revenue and profit move in opposite directions.

[3]

(d)

Determine the number of members the gym would need at the new monthly fee to leave its monthly profit unchanged, and compare that number with the $360$ members the manager expects.

[3]

(e)

Evaluate whether Highfield Fitness should cut its monthly fee, referring both to the figures you have calculated and to the assumptions behind the manager's expectation.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Current monthly revenue:
$$300 \times \u00a340 = \u00a312{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
Contribution per member is the price less the variable cost of serving that member:
$$\u00a340 - \u00a36 = \u00a334 \;\; (A1).$$
Total monthly contribution is $300 \times \u00a334 = \u00a310{,}200$, and after fixed costs the monthly profit is
$$\u00a310{,}200 - \u00a38{,}000 = \u00a32{,}200 \;\; (A1).$$
Note that the $£6$ per member is a *variable* cost: it is incurred only for members the gym actually has, which is why it is deducted from the price rather than lumped with the rent.

(b) The proposal changes the price by $-15\%$ and, on the manager's own figure, changes the quantity demanded by $+20\%$. So
$$\text{PED} = \frac{\text{percentage change in quantity demanded}}{\text{percentage change in price}} = \frac{+20\%}{-15\%} = -1.33 \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
The *magnitude* is greater than one, $|{-1.33}| > 1$, so demand is price-elastic over this range $(A1)$. That is exactly the condition the manager is relying on: with elastic demand, a fall in price raises total revenue. The candidate should be able to state that conclusion and it is correct.

(c) At the new fee the gym has $300 \times 1.20 = 360$ members and charges $\u00a340 \times 0.85 = \u00a334$, so
$$\text{new revenue} = 360 \times \u00a334 = \u00a312{,}240,$$
a rise of $\u00a3240$ a month on the $£12{,}000$ in part (a) $(A1)$.

Profit falls, however, because the contribution per member falls with the price while the variable cost does not. The new contribution per member is $\u00a334 - \u00a36 = \u00a328$, so
$$\text{new total contribution} = 360 \times \u00a328 = \u00a310{,}080,$$
and
$$\text{new profit} = \u00a310{,}080 - \u00a38{,}000 = \u00a32{,}080 \;\; (A1).$$
That is $\u00a3120$ *less* than the present profit of $\u00a32{,}200$.

Revenue and profit move in opposite directions because they are governed by different quantities $(A1)$. Revenue depends only on price times volume, and elasticity is precisely a statement about revenue; profit depends on the *contribution* each member makes, and the six-pound cut in price cuts contribution per member by the same six pounds, from $\u00a334$ to $\u00a328$, a fall of $17.6\%$. A $20\%$ rise in volume cannot offset a fall of that size in contribution per unit, so the total contribution falls even though the revenue rises. Elasticity is silent about profit because it works with revenue alone; the variable cost is what breaks the coincidence between the two.

(d) To hold profit where it is, the new total contribution must still be $\u00a310{,}200$, so the gym needs
$$\frac{\u00a310{,}200}{\u00a328} = 364.3 \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
Membership comes in whole numbers, so the gym would need $365$ members $(A1)$. The manager expects $360$ members, which is five short of the membership required, and at $360$ members the profit is the $\u00a32{,}080$ of part (c). The comparison to state is that the proposal misses its own break-even point by about five memberships, not that it is close to it: five members is a small number of people but it is the whole of the margin.

(e) On the figures given, the gym should not cut the fee. The decision is not close: every member the gym gains at $\u00a334$ adds $\u00a328$ of contribution, and the fee cut removes $\u00a36$ of contribution from each of the $300$ members who would have paid $\u00a340$ anyway. The gain from fifty more members (about $360 - 300 = 60$ extra, worth $60 \times \u00a328 = \u00a31{,}680$) is outweighed by the $300 \times \u00a36 = \u00a31{,}800$ given up on the members who were already there $(A1)$, and the two figures have been arranged so that this is exactly the $\u00a3120$ shortfall. A cut of this size cannot pay for itself unless almost every existing member stays and the new members arrive in numbers the trial does not promise.

The weaknesses in the manager's expectation should be identified rather than assumed away $(A1)$. The $20\%$ figure comes from a *neighbouring town*, so it is evidence about a different location, a different competing set of gyms and a different population; the manager's belief that it would hold here is an assumption, not a measurement $(A1)$. The trial also tells the manager what happened to membership when the price was cut elsewhere, with no indication of how long the effect lasted; a promotional price often attracts members who leave when it rises, which would raise the variable-cost base without building the membership the gym wants.

A judgement is required, and it should be a clear one $(A1)$. The strongest honest case for the cut is not in the figures but beside them: if the extra members raise the gym's utilisation, its classes fill, its atmosphere improves and its retention improves, then part of the benefit would appear *later* in lower turnover among existing members, which the item's numbers do not capture. That argument is real, but it is not what the manager offered, and it would have to be large enough to close a gap of at least $\u00a3120$ a month and probably much more. On the arithmetic presented, the recommendation is to keep the fee at $\u00a340$ and look elsewhere for the members: the gym has $200$ memberships of headroom and the cheapest way to fill them is not to reduce the contribution of the members it already has.
questions.explanation:
This item is built around the single most common error in pricing work, which is to answer a revenue question when a profit question was asked. The two are not the same, and the difference between them is a variable cost.

Price elasticity of demand is a statement about revenue, and it is a good one: if the magnitude is greater than one, a fall in price raises total revenue, and the numbers here are arranged so that this is true. The manager is not wrong about that at all -- revenue does rise, from $\u00a312{,}000$ to $£12{,}240$ a month. A candidate who stops at that point has done the elasticity correctly and has still given the wrong answer, because the proposal has to be judged on profit, and profit depends on contribution per unit, not on revenue.

The arithmetic that separates them is one line long. Cutting the price by $£6$ cuts the contribution of every member by $£6$, from $\u00a334$ to $\u00a328$; a $£6$ cut on $300$ members costs $\u00a31{,}800$ a month in contribution on the very members the gym already has, and the $60$ new members contribute $60 \times \u00a328 = \u00a31{,}680$. The gap is the $\u00a3120$ by which profit falls, and it is not a rounding error or a modelling artefact: it is the whole point. Elasticity could not have caught it, because elasticity compares percentage changes and does not know that the price has a cost underneath it.

Part (d) turns the same arithmetic into a target. The membership that holds profit is $31$ more than the forecast, so the proposal fails by five members, which sounds trivial and is not: the gym would have to reach $365$ members to stand still, and the trial it is relying on promises $360$. The distinction between "almost break-even" and "short of break-even" is the distinction between a project that should be reconsidered with better research and one that should be refused on the present numbers.

Only the evaluation part opens the qualitative door, and it is deliberately narrow. There is a genuine argument for the cut -- a fuller gym is a better gym, and happier existing members are less likely to leave -- but it is not the argument the manager made, and it does not appear anywhere in the figures. The mark is for noticing that the honest counter-argument rests on retention benefits the item has not quantified, and for refusing to let the assumption of a $20\%$ response from another town carry a decision worth more than the gap it has to close.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 2.1 The cost of labour turnover against the cost of a retention pay rise, where the wrong comparison is total recruitment spend against total salary increase rather than the saving the proposal actually buys
questions.command_term: Calculate, Calculate, Show that, Determine, Evaluate
questions.question:
The directors of a call centre are considering a pay rise in order to keep staff. Using the figures in the stimulus, calculate the present turnover rate and the present annual recruitment cost; calculate the annual cost of the proposed pay rise; show what the pay rise would save and what it would add; determine how many leavers it would have to prevent to pay for itself; and evaluate whether the pay rise should be approved.

(a)

Calculate the number of staff who left in the year just ended, the present annual cost of recruitment and training, and express the turnover rate as it is normally stated.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the annual cost of the proposed $4\%$ pay rise across the whole workforce.

[3]

(c)

Show that if the pay rise did halve the turnover rate it would save $£150{,}000$ a year in recruitment and training, and that against its own cost this increases the call centre's total annual costs by $£202{,}000$.

[3]

(d)

Determine how many leavers the pay rise would have to prevent in a year in order to pay for itself, and compare that number with the total number of leavers at the present turnover rate.

[3]

(e)

Evaluate whether the directors should approve the pay rise, referring to the figures you have calculated and to the assumptions on which the human resource manager's expectation rests.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) A turnover rate of $30\%$ on a workforce of $400$ means
$$400 \times 0.30 = 120 \;\; (A1)$$
staff left during the year. At $£2{,}500$ to recruit and train one replacement, the present annual cost of turnover is
$$120 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3300{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The turnover rate is already stated as a percentage of the workforce, so it is $30\%$; it may also be expressed as $120$ leavers against an average workforce of $400$, which is the same figure $(A1)$. It is worth noting that the $£300{,}000$ is money the call centre is *already* spending, not a new cost, and that nothing in the pay rise changes it except by changing the number of leavers.

(b) A $4\%$ rise on an average salary of $£22{,}000$ is
$$\u00a322{,}000 \times 0.04 = \u00a3880 \;\; (M1)$$
per member of staff per year. Across $400$ staff this is
$$400 \times \u00a3880 = \u00a3352{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The whole of that $\u00a3352{,}000$ is a new, recurring cost $(A1)$: it is paid every year for as long as the pay rate stands, and it is paid to all $400$ staff, not only to the ones the rise is meant to keep.

(c) If turnover halved, from $30\%$ to $15\%$, the number of leavers would fall from $120$ to $400 \times 0.15 = 60$. The saving is the cost of the $60$ replacements the call centre no longer needs:
$$(120 - 60) \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3150{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The pay rise costs $\u00a3352{,}000$. The change in the call centre's total costs is therefore
$$+\u00a3352{,}000 - \u00a3150{,}000 = +\u00a3202{,}000,$$
a rise of $\u00a3202{,}000$ a year $(A1)$, not a saving. Put as totals: recruitment and training would fall to $60 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3150{,}000$, and with the new salary bill of $\u00a3352{,}000$ sitting on top of it the two costs together come to about $\u00a3502{,}000$ against the present $\u00a3300{,}000$ $(A1)$.

The essential point is which quantity changes. The present turnover cost of $\u00a3300{,}000$ does not become zero when turnover halves; it becomes $\u00a3150{,}000$. The proposal buys a *reduction* of $\u00a3150{,}000$, and it must be set against a cost of $\u00a3352{,}000$, not against the $\u00a3300{,}000$ that was being spent anyway.

(d) To pay for itself, the recruitment saving must equal the cost of the rise, so the number of replacements the rise must prevent is
$$\frac{\u00a3352{,}000}{\u00a32{,}500} = 140.8 \;\; (M1)(A1),$$
that is $141$ leavers must be prevented. But at the present turnover rate only $120$ staff leave in a whole year, so there are not $141$ leavers to prevent: even a turnover rate of zero would remove only $120$ replacements and save $120 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3300{,}000$, which is $£52{,}000$ short of the cost of the rise $(A1)$. The conclusion is sharp and worth stating plainly: on the figures given, the pay rise cannot pay for itself at any turnover rate, because its maximum possible saving is smaller than its cost.

(e) On the arithmetic, the directors should not approve the rise as a way of saving money, because it does the opposite: it adds $\u00a3202{,}000$ a year to costs even while delivering the halving of turnover the manager expects $(A1)$. The maximum saving available from the whole of the call centre's turnover problem is $\u00a3300{,}000$, and the rise costs $\u00a3352{,}000$, so the retention case cannot be made on recruitment savings at all -- the manager's mechanism fails before any assumption is tested.

The assumption should then be examined on its own terms $(A1)$. Halving turnover from $30\%$ to $15\%$ is a very large change to attribute to a pay rise of $4\%$, and the evidence for it is that pay is what leavers *say* in exit interviews; what people say when they leave is not the same as what would have kept them. A $4\%$ rise is below the level of inflation in most years, so it may not even be felt as a real improvement. If the manager is optimistic and turnover falls by less than half, the saving shrinks further while the $\u00a3352{,}000$ does not.

A judgement is still required, and there is an honest case on the other side $(A1)$. The figures only cover salary and recruitment, and the directors explicitly did not ask about anything else; turnover also carries a cost in service quality, in the loss of experienced agents, and in the morale of the staff who remain, none of which is in the $£2{,}500$ figure. If those costs are large, a pay rise could be justified as a *service* investment rather than a *recruitment* saving -- but that is a different argument from the one the manager made, and it would have to be supported by evidence the call centre has not gathered.

The recommendation should be direct $(A1)$. Approve no pay rise on the case as put, because the retention argument is arithmetically impossible: a rise costing $\u00a3352{,}000$ cannot recover more than $\u00a3300{,}000$ in avoided recruitment even if nobody left. If the directors want to reduce turnover, a smaller, targeted measure -- a retention bonus paid only to staff who stay, or an increase confined to the roles that actually leave -- would cost less than a rise paid to all $400$ and would not repeat every year for the staff it is not needed for.
questions.explanation:
The trap in this item is a comparison that looks natural and is wrong. Presented with a recruitment bill of $£300{,}000$ and a proposed pay rise of $£352{,}000$, almost everyone's first move is to set the two side by side, and the two are so close that the pay rise appears to be very nearly self-financing. The manager's case then seems to rest on the small gap, and the retention benefit is assumed to close it.

The comparison is invalid because the $£300{,}000$ is not what the pay rise saves. It is what the call centre is already spending, and it would still be spending a good part of it if the rise were approved, because halving turnover does not abolish recruitment; it halves it. What the proposal actually buys is the difference between two recruitment bills, and that difference is $£150{,}000$ against a salary increase of $£352{,}000$. This is the total-versus-marginal confusion in its most common business form, and it is worth more than the arithmetic that exposes it.

Part (d) then closes the escape that a candidate who has understood part (c) might still look for. If the pay rise falls short by $£202{,}000$, the obvious next thought is that a bigger fall in turnover would close the gap. It would not. The call centre has $120$ leavers a year; preventing every single one of them, which means a turnover rate of zero, saves $£300{,}000$, and the rise costs $£352{,}000$. The target of $141$ leavers prevented simply does not exist in a workforce that loses $120$ people. The proposal fails structurally, not marginally, and the difference between those two verdicts is what the part is for.

The evaluation mark sits on top of that. There is a real argument for paying staff more -- turnover damages service quality and drains experience in ways the $£2{,}500$ figure does not price -- and a good answer may make it. But it must make it honestly, as a service investment whose benefits are outside the arithmetic, rather than dressing it up as a saving the numbers refute. The stimulus is deliberately explicit that the directors asked only about recruitment and salary, so a candidate who invents other savings to rescue the proposal is answering a question that was not asked.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 4.4 Purchase-intent research read with 6.7 weighted and standardised rates
questions.question:
Nordvik Drinks commissions two waves of purchase-intent research for a new low-sugar cordial. Respondents are asked whether they would definitely or probably buy the product at its intended price.

Wave 1 is an in-store intercept survey carried out at weekends. Wave 2 is an online panel carried out on weekdays.

The company's target market for the launch is 900 000 adults, split 30% / 40% / 30% between the 18–34, 35–54 and 55+ bands. Each buyer is expected to make one purchase in the launch year, and the gross margin is £1.40 per unit.

(a)

Calculate the overall positive response rate for each wave.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the positive response rate within each of the three age bands for each wave, and state what your results show that the comparison in part (a) conceals.

[4]

(c)

Using the target market mix of 30% / 40% / 30%, show that the age-standardised positive rate is 25.0% for wave 1 and 30.0% for wave 2.

[4]

(d)

The marketing director proposes to forecast launch-year sales using the wave 2 overall rate from part (a). Evaluate this proposal, quantifying its effect on the launch decision.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Wave 1: $\dfrac{118}{400} \times 100 = 29.5\%$. Wave 2: $\dfrac{153}{600} \times 100 = 25.5\%$. On this comparison purchase intent appears to have fallen by $4.0$ percentage points between the two waves.

(b) Wave 1. 18–34: $\dfrac{80}{200} = 40.0\%$. 35–54: $\dfrac{30}{120} = 25.0\%$. 55+: $\dfrac{8}{80} = 10.0\%$.

Wave 2. 18–34: $\dfrac{54}{120} = 45.0\%$. 35–54: $\dfrac{54}{180} = 30.0\%$. 55+: $\dfrac{45}{300} = 15.0\%$.

Intent rose in every single band — by 5.0, 5.0 and 5.0 percentage points respectively. The overall comparison in part (a) conceals this completely, because the two waves did not interview the same mix of people: wave 2 drew 300 of its 600 respondents from the 55+ band, against 80 of 400 in wave 1, and that band has the lowest intent in both waves. The headline fall is an artefact of who was asked, not a change in what people think.

(c) Applying the target mix to the wave 1 band rates: $0.30(40.0) + 0.40(25.0) + 0.30(10.0) = 12.0 + 10.0 + 3.0 = 25.0\%$. Applying it to the wave 2 band rates: $0.30(45.0) + 0.40(30.0) + 0.30(15.0) = 13.5 + 12.0 + 4.5 = 30.0\%$. Both waves are therefore reweighted onto the same population, and on that like-for-like basis intent rose by $5.0$ percentage points.

(d) The proposal should be rejected. The wave 2 overall rate of 25.5% is computed on a sample that is not representative of the target market: it over-weights the 55+ band by a factor of roughly five relative to the target mix. Applying it gives $900\,000 \times 0.255 = 229\,500$ buyers. Applying the standardised wave 2 rate of 30.0% gives $900\,000 \times 0.30 = 270\,000$ buyers. The difference is $40\,500$ units, and at a gross margin of £1.40 that is $40\,500 \times 1.40 = £56\,700$ of margin left out of the forecast. That is large enough to change the decision if the launch has a fixed cost close to the projected margin — a project that looks marginal at 229 500 units may clear its threshold at 270 000. Against this, the standardised figure is not free of doubt: wave 2 was an online panel taken on weekdays, so it may under-represent people who shop in stores at weekends, and stated purchase intent reliably overstates actual buying. The defensible conclusion is that the director's method is wrong in a known direction and by a known amount, and that the forecast should use the standardised rate while being presented as an upper estimate.
questions.explanation:
This is a descriptive-statistics item in which the obvious statistic is the wrong one. Both headline rates are arithmetically correct — 29.5% and 25.5% — and both are misleading, because the denominator changed shape between the waves. Wave 2 interviewed 300 over-55s out of 600; wave 1 interviewed 80 out of 400. Since that band is the least enthusiastic in both waves, moving it from a fifth to a half of the sample drags the overall figure down even though enthusiasm went up everywhere.

The skill being tested is knowing which tool to reach for. A simple overall rate is the right tool for a representative sample and the wrong tool for two samples with different compositions; the right tool here is a standardised rate, which reweights each wave onto the same reference population. Once that is done the sign of the change flips: the raw comparison says intent fell by 4.0 points, and the standardised comparison says it rose by 5.0. That reversal is not a curiosity — it is the whole decision, because the forecast built on the raw figure is short by 40 500 buyers and £56 700 of margin.

The most common error is to pool the two waves into a single sample of 1 000 and quote 27.1%, which combines the two sampling biases rather than removing either. A second is to notice that the samples differ but then adjust in the wrong direction, or to dismiss wave 2 entirely as 'biased' without recognising that both waves can be used once they are standardised. A third, subtler, error is to treat the standardised 30.0% as a reliable forecast in itself: stated purchase intent is systematically optimistic, and the online weekday panel carries its own coverage problem. The best answers quantify the director's error and then say what the corrected figure is still worth.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 3.5 When the ratios improve and the cash position does not: a financing decision the numbers cannot settle
questions.question:
Ravensworth Ltd is a wholesaler. Extracts from its accounts for two years are shown below, together with the figures for a proposed expansion.

| | Year 1 (\$000) | Year 2 (\$000) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 2 400 | 3 200 |
| Gross profit | 900 | 1 120 |
| Net profit before interest and tax | 288 | 352 |
| Capital employed | 1 800 | 1 920 |
| Inventory | 300 | 420 |
| Other current assets | 320 | 280 |
| Current liabilities | 310 | 500 |

The directors propose an expansion costing \$180 000, which would be financed entirely by an increase in the bank overdraft. The expansion would increase inventory by \$180 000 and is expected to raise annual net profit before interest and tax by \$46 000. No other figure in the table would change immediately.

(a)

For each of Year 1 and Year 2, calculate the gross profit margin, the net profit margin, the return on capital employed and the current ratio. Give ratios to two decimal places and percentages to one decimal place.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the acid test ratio for each year. Hence analyse whether the financial performance of Ravensworth Ltd improved in Year 2.

[4]

(c)

Calculate, for the proposed expansion: the annual percentage return on the \$180 000 invested, the payback period, and the current ratio and acid test ratio immediately after the expansion is financed by the overdraft.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate whether the directors should proceed with the expansion on the terms described. There is no single correct answer: marks are awarded for the reasoning, including the use of the figures you have calculated.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Year 1 (A1 for the year):

  • Gross profit margin $= 900 \div 2400 = 37.5\%$
  • Net profit margin $= 288 \div 2400 = 12.0\%$
  • Return on capital employed $= 288 \div 1800 = 16.0\%$
  • Current ratio $= (300 + 320) \div 310 = 620 \div 310 = 2.00$

Year 2 (A1 for the year):

  • Gross profit margin $= 1120 \div 3200 = 35.0\%$
  • Net profit margin $= 352 \div 3200 = 11.0\%$
  • Return on capital employed $= 352 \div 1920 = 18.3\%$
  • Current ratio $= (420 + 280) \div 500 = 700 \div 500 = 1.40$

One mark is available for each of the four ratios being correct in both years (A1 each).

(b) The acid test ratio is $320 \div 310 = 1.03$ for Year 1 and $280 \div 500 = 0.56$ for Year 2 (A1).

The assessment has to be given in two directions, and a candidate who gives only one of them has not finished (A1). Profitability as a return on the resources employed improved: ROCE rose from $16.0\%$ to $18.3\%$ and absolute net profit rose from \$288 000 to \$352 000 (A1). But profitability as a margin, and liquidity, both deteriorated: gross margin fell from $37.5\%$ to $35.0\%$, net margin from $12.0\%$ to $11.0\%$, the current ratio from $2.00$ to $1.40$, and the acid test ratio from $1.03$ to $0.56$ (A1).

The acid test figure is the one that matters. At $0.56$ the business cannot cover its current liabilities out of current assets without selling inventory, and the fall from $1.03$ to $0.56$ means it has moved from comfortable to exposed in a single year. The most likely explanation is that rapid revenue growth of $33\%$ has been financed by current liabilities, which rose from \$310 000 to \$500 000, rather than by new capital.

(c) Annual return $= 46 000 \div 180 000 = 25.6\%$ (A1). Payback period $= 180 000 \div 46 000 = 3.9$ years (A1).

After the expansion, financed by the overdraft: other current assets stay at \$280 000, inventory rises to $420 + 180 = \$600 000$, so current assets total \$880 000; current liabilities rise to $500 + 180 = \$680 000$.

  • Current ratio $= 880 \div 680 = 1.29$ (A1)
  • Acid test ratio $= (880 - 600) \div 680 = 280 \div 680 = 0.41$ (A1)

(d) A developed answer distinguishes the project from the method of finance, and that is the insight the item is built around (A1).

The project looks sound on its own terms. A return of $25.6\%$ exceeds the current ROCE of $18.3\%$, so the expansion would raise the average return on capital employed, and a payback period of $3.9$ years is reasonable for a wholesaler investing in stock-holding capacity. On the quantitative evidence alone the expansion earns more than it costs.

The method of finance does not. Overdraft finance is repayable on demand and is a current liability, so it pushes the current ratio down from $1.40$ to $1.29$ and the acid test ratio from $0.56$ to $0.41$ (A1). At $0.41$ the business would be holding \$600 000 of inventory against \$680 000 of liabilities falling due within the year, and the additional inventory is precisely the asset the acid test excludes. Financing a three-to-four-year investment with money that can be recalled at short notice is a maturity mismatch, and the ratios are right to flag it.

The conclusion candidates should reach is that the expansion should proceed but should not be financed this way. If the same \$180 000 were raised as a long-term loan, current liabilities would stay at \$500 000 and the current ratio would be $880 \div 500 = 1.76$, with the acid test ratio unchanged at $0.56$ -- that is, the expansion would improve the current ratio rather than damage it. The objection is to the overdraft, not to the investment (A1).

A candidate who reaches the opposite conclusion -- that the business should not expand at all -- can still be credited fully if the judgement is supported by the figures, for example by arguing that an acid test ratio of $0.56$ before any expansion is already too low to take on further fixed commitments, and that the business should rebuild liquidity first. What earns no credit is letting the $25.6\%$ return settle the question on its own, because that number is silent about when the money has to be repaid.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the arithmetic and the answer pull in different directions, and the gap between them is the whole question. Part (c) produces a return of $25.6\%$ against a current ROCE of $18.3\%$ and a payback of $3.9$ years. Every one of those numbers says yes. Part (c) also produces an acid test ratio of $0.41$, and that number says no. A candidate who stops at the first set has done the calculation and missed the decision.

What makes it a judgement rather than a tie-break is that the conflict is not between two estimates of the same thing -- it is between two different questions. The return and the payback ask whether the expansion is worth doing. The liquidity ratios ask whether it can be survived. Both are legitimate, and neither reduces to the other. The candidate has to hold them together long enough to see that they are not actually in conflict about the same object: the expansion is fine, the overdraft is not, and financing the one with the other is the single decision that is wrong.

That is why the answer rewards the long-term-finance comparison even though it is not asked for. Recomputing the current ratio at $1.76$ under a loan settles the matter in a way no amount of argument can: the project improves liquidity when it is financed properly, so the objection was never to the project. This is the move the item is looking for, and it is a genuinely IB move -- using a second quantitative scenario to test a qualitative conclusion.

There is also a quieter trap in part (b). ROCE rises while both margins fall, and the absolute profit rises while the percentage earned on each dollar of revenue falls. Candidates read 'profit went up' as 'performance improved' and stop. The figures are arranged so that the opposite reading is equally available, and the mark scheme rewards holding both.

This is adapted from the UK A-level Business treatment of ratio analysis, where a two-year comparison is followed by an evaluative judgement on a proposed investment. The A-level version typically asks simply whether the business should proceed. Here the proposal is specified as overdraft-financed and the inventory treatment is made explicit, so that the liquidity effect can be calculated rather than asserted, and the mark scheme credits the alternative financing comparison -- which the source does not require.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 3.8 Investment appraisal
questions.question:
The two projects are mutually exclusive, so Kestrel Leisure can accept at most one of them.

(a)

Calculate the payback period of each project, giving your answers in years to two decimal places.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the average rate of return of each project, using average annual profit as a percentage of the initial investment.

[3]

(c)

Using the discount factors provided, calculate the net present value of each project.

[4]

(d)

Recalculate the net present value of Project B to include the working capital requirement, and then recommend which project Kestrel Leisure should accept. Justify your recommendation using all of your calculations.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Project A. Cumulative cash flow: after Year 1, €120 000; after Year 2, €280 000; after Year 3, €460 000. The investment of €400 000 is recovered during Year 3, when €120 000 of the €180 000 inflow is still needed. (M1)

Payback $=2+\dfrac{120\,000}{180\,000}=2.67$ years. (A1)

Project B. Cumulative cash flow: after Year 1, €60 000; after Year 2, €160 000; after Year 3, €320 000; after Year 4, €560 000. The investment is recovered during Year 4, when €80 000 of the €240 000 inflow is still needed. (M1)

Payback $=3+\dfrac{80\,000}{240\,000}=3.33$ years. (A1)

(b) Project A: total net cash flow is $120\,000+160\,000+180\,000+80\,000=540\,000$, so total profit is $540\,000-400\,000=140\,000$ and average annual profit is $\dfrac{140\,000}{4}=35\,000$. (M1)

ARR $=\dfrac{35\,000}{400\,000}\times 100=8.75\%$. (A1)

Project B: total net cash flow is €560 000, so total profit is €160 000 and average annual profit is $\dfrac{160\,000}{4}=40\,000$. ARR $=\dfrac{40\,000}{400\,000}\times 100=10.00\%$. (A1)

(c) Project A: the present values of the inflows are $120\,000(0.909)=109\,080$; $160\,000(0.826)=132\,160$; $180\,000(0.751)=135\,180$; and $80\,000(0.683)=54\,640$. The total present value is €431 060. (M1)(A1)

NPV of A $=431\,060-400\,000=+€31\,060$. (A1)

Project B: the present values are $60\,000(0.909)=54\,540$; $100\,000(0.826)=82\,600$; $160\,000(0.751)=120\,160$; and $240\,000(0.683)=163\,920$, totalling €421 220. NPV of B $=421\,220-400\,000=+€21\,220$. (A1)

(d) Project B also requires €50 000 of working capital at the start, an immediate outflow that must be discounted at the Year 0 factor of 1.000, and it recovers €50 000 at the end of Year 4, whose present value is $50\,000(0.683)=34\,150$. (M1)

Revised NPV of B $=421\,220-400\,000-50\,000+34\,150=+€5\,370$. (A1)

Recommendation: accept Project A. (A1)

Justification: Project A is superior on two of the three methods. It pays back in 2.67 years against 3.33, which matters because the loan is being serviced at 10% and a shorter payback shortens the period during which the company carries the risk of the cash flows not materialising. Its NPV is €31 060 against €5 370 for Project B once the working capital is included, and since the money is borrowed at exactly the 10% used to discount, the NPV is the method that measures the effect on shareholder wealth directly. Project B is only superior on ARR, at 10.00% against 8.75%, and that measure is misleading here because it ignores the timing of the cash flows and, as presented, ignores the working capital entirely. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The three methods produce a genuine disagreement, and the disagreement is the question. Project A is better on payback and, once the working capital is included, overwhelmingly better on NPV; Project B is better on ARR. A student who treats the three methods as interchangeable will not be able to recommend anything, because no single method ranks the projects in isolation from the company's circumstances.

The way through is to ask what the money costs. Kestrel Leisure is borrowing at 10%, and that is exactly the rate used to discount, so the NPV is measuring the effect of the investment on the value of the company after the lender has been paid. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the loan costs; a NPV of €5 370 on a €450 000 commitment is barely positive, which means Project B is close to being value-destroying once the working capital is properly accounted for. The payback figure tells the same story from the risk side: a company with debt wants cash back quickly, and Project A returns the investment almost two-thirds of a year sooner.

ARR is the odd one out, and it is worth being able to say why. It is an accounting measure that averages the profits over the life of the project, so it treats €240 000 received in Year 4 as though it were as valuable as €240 000 received in Year 1. It also ignores the working capital unless the candidate chooses to include it, and it takes no account of the size or timing of the cash flows. Here it flatters Project B precisely because B's cash flows come late and are large, which is the opposite of what a company servicing a loan should want.

The working-capital adjustment is where the question stops being routine. Working capital is not an expense: it is cash paid out that comes back. Discounting the recovery is what makes the arithmetic honest, because €50 000 returned in four years is worth €34 150 today. Students who treat the whole €50 000 as a cost will reject Project B for the wrong reason, and students who ignore it entirely will recommend it for the wrong reason.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Location
questions.question:
Tarn Valley Preserves must commit to one site, and the choice will be difficult to reverse because the lease runs for ten years.

(a)

Calculate the total annual cost at each site if demand is 220 000 units, and state which site is cheaper.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the output at which the total annual costs of the two sites are equal.

[3]

(c)

Using the probabilities given, calculate the expected annual cost at each site and comment on what your answer means for the decision.

[4]

(d)

Recommend which site Tarn Valley Preserves should choose, justifying your answer with reference to your calculations and to two qualitative factors.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Site X: total cost $=280\,000+1.80(220\,000)=280\,000+396\,000=€676\,000$. (M1)(A1)

Site Y: total cost $=140\,000+2.60(220\,000)=140\,000+572\,000=€712\,000$. (A1)

Site X is cheaper by €36 000 per year at this level of demand. (A1)

(b) Setting the two total costs equal: $280\,000+1.80q=140\,000+2.60q$. (M1)

So $140\,000=0.80q$ and $q=175\,000$ units. (M1)(A1)

Site Y is cheaper below this output and Site X above it, because Site X trades higher fixed costs for a lower variable cost per unit.

(c) Site X: $0.6(676\,000)+0.4(496\,000)=405\,600+198\,400=€604\,000$. (M1)(A1)

Site Y: $0.6(712\,000)+0.4(452\,000)=427\,200+180\,800=€608\,000$. (A1)

The expected costs differ by only €4000 per year on a commitment of more than half a million euros per year, which is well under 1% of the total. (A1) The expected-value calculation therefore does not settle the question: whichever site is chosen, the company is making almost the same bet on cost, and the decision will be decided by which risk the management team is more willing to carry rather than by the arithmetic. It is also worth noting that the expected value conceals the shape of the risk: Site Y is cheaper in the low-demand outcome and more expensive in the high-demand outcome, so choosing Y is choosing to be relatively safe if demand disappoints, while Site X is choosing to be better off if demand materialises.

(d) Recommendation: choose Site X, the city centre. (A1)

The quantitative case is narrow but consistent: Site X is €36 000 per year cheaper at the higher demand level, it has the lower expected cost at €604 000 against €608 000, and its crossover point of 175 000 units sits well below the 220 000 units that marketing considers more likely than not. Since the lease runs for ten years and the higher-demand outcome is the one the company's growth plan depends on, the cheaper variable cost is the more valuable characteristic to lock in. (A1)

The decisive qualitative factor is space. Site X has no room to expand at any price, so if demand exceeds 220 000 units the company would have to acquire a second site and duplicate management, which would destroy most of the cost advantage it has just calculated. Site Y has a large plot available now, which gives the business the option to grow without a second location. (A1)

The counter-argument is labour. Site X has a large local pool of skilled production staff, while Site Y would require training, which adds cost and time and creates a dependency on retaining the staff it trains. A preserves manufacturer depends on consistent product quality, so the availability of experienced staff reduces operational risk. On balance the expected cost difference is too small to decide the matter, and the choice between the two risks comes down to which the company fears more: a permanent capacity ceiling on a growing product, or an operating cost it cannot control. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The crossover calculation is the centre of the question and it is easy to perform mechanically without noticing what it does. There is a level of output at which the two sites cost the same, and below it the site with the lower fixed cost wins while above it the site with the lower variable cost wins. Writing that conclusion explicitly is what turns a calculation into analysis, and it is what most candidates omit.

The more interesting feature is the expected value. It is a legitimate technique and the numbers are easy, but the answer it gives is a €4000 difference on annual costs of more than €600 000, which is less than the uncertainty in any of the underlying estimates. A number that precise, resting on probabilities that are themselves a judgement, cannot bear the weight of a ten-year decision. Recognising that a calculation can be correct and still not be decisive is the analytical step the question is testing, and it is the difference between a candidate who uses a tool and one who is used by it.

That is why the qualitative factors do the real work. The decisive one is the absence of expansion space at Site X. Ten years is a long commitment for a business whose management believes demand is more likely to rise than to fall, and a site with a hard capacity ceiling turns success into a problem. The labour factor pulls the other way and a strong answer will acknowledge it rather than ignore it. The judgement is not about which factor is objectively more important but about which risk the business is better placed to absorb: a company that is already short of space is likely to value the option to expand more than a modest reduction in the risk of training costs.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.2 Operations methods
questions.question:
Hartswood Garden Furniture must decide whether to invest EUR 600 000 in a flow production line for its best-selling bench.

(a)

Explain two reasons why the consultant believes flow production would be suitable for the bench, and one reason why the company's other eleven products make flow production difficult.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the mean monthly demand for the bench and the demand in a peak month. Calculate the unit cost of the bench under batch production and under flow production at an annual volume of 48 000 units, and comment on the difference.

[5]

(c)

Using descriptive statistics and a decision tree, evaluate whether Hartswood should invest in the flow production line. Justify your answer with reference to capacity, storage cost and the product range.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The consultant's case for flow production rests on volume and cost. The bench is a single, standardised product made in large numbers - 48 000 units a year - and flow production is designed for exactly this: a continuous sequence of operations with little or no changeover, which spreads a high fixed cost over a large output and gives a low variable cost. Second, demand for the bench is predictable in total, and the consultant argues that a dedicated line would remove the batch changeovers that currently interrupt production. (A1)(A1)

The eleven other products are the problem. Flow production is only economic when a line can run for long periods without being stopped and altered. Hartswood makes twelve variants in total, and a flow line for the bench cannot make tables, chairs or the other bench designs. Those products must stay on batch production, so the investment would improve the cost of one product out of twelve while leaving the rest of the factory unchanged. (A1)(A1)

(b) Mean monthly demand $= 48 000 / 12 = 4 000$ benches. (A1)

Peak demand: 80% of 48 000 $= 38 400$ benches are sold in three months, so peak monthly demand $= 38 400 / 3 = 12 800$ benches. (M1)(A1)

Unit cost at 48 000 units:

Batch: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 180 000 / 48 000 = EUR 3.75$; plus variable cost EUR 18.25, giving EUR 22.00 per bench. (M1)(A1)
Flow: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 480 000 / 48 000 = EUR 10.00$; plus variable cost EUR 10.00, giving EUR 20.00 per bench. (A1)

Comment: at 48 000 units flow production is EUR 2.00 a bench cheaper, a saving of EUR 96 000 a year, and the crossover point at which flow becomes cheaper is $(EUR 480 000 - EUR 180 000) / (EUR 18.25 - EUR 10.00) = 36 364$ benches. Since annual demand is 48 000, the arithmetic appears to favour flow - but this comparison ignores the constraint that the flow line's capacity of 8 000 benches a month imposes on a seasonal product.

(c) Indicative evaluation, using descriptive statistics and a decision tree.

The descriptive statistics show why the annual average is the wrong basis for the decision. Mean monthly demand is 4 000 benches, but peak monthly demand is 12 800 and off-season demand is about 1 067. The range is therefore about 11 733 benches a month. The flow line can make only 8 000 a month, so in each of the three peak months it is short by $12 800 - 8 000 = 4 800$ benches. Over the three months the shortfall is 14 400 benches, all of which must be made in advance and stored. (M1)(A1)

Storage costs EUR 3 a bench a month, and the consultant expects an average holding period of four months: $14 400 \times EUR 3 \times 4 = EUR 172 800$ a year. The EUR 96 000 saving from flow production is therefore more than wiped out, leaving flow production EUR 76 800 a year more expensive than batch at the higher demand level. (A1)

The decision tree makes the same point under uncertainty. Marketing estimates a 0.6 probability that demand is 48 000 and a 0.4 probability that it is 30 000.

Batch production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 18.25 \times 48 000 = EUR 1 056 000$; at 30 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 547 500 = EUR 727 500$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 056 000 + 0.4 \times EUR 727 500 = EUR 924 600$. (M1)(A1)

Flow production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 10 \times 48 000 = EUR 960 000$, plus storage of EUR 172 800, giving EUR 1 132 800. At 30 000, peak monthly demand is $0.8 \times 30 000 / 3 = 8 000$, which exactly equals the line's capacity, so no storage is needed and cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 300 000 = EUR 780 000$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 132 800 + 0.4 \times EUR 780 000 = EUR 991 680$. (M1)(A1)

Batch production has the lower expected cost, by EUR 67 080, and the conclusion does not depend on the probabilities: flow is more expensive in the high-demand state and also more expensive in the low-demand state, so no plausible weighting reverses it.

The flow line would also commit EUR 600 000, would be difficult to change over, and could not make the other eleven products. Conclusion: Hartswood should not invest in the flow line. A stronger answer will note that the same analysis would justify revisiting flow production if the company could smooth demand, reduce the product range, or add a second line to raise peak capacity.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the obvious quantitative answer is the wrong one. At 48 000 units a year the flow line costs EUR 20 a bench against EUR 22 for batch, a saving of EUR 96 000, and the crossover point of 36 364 benches is comfortably below the annual volume. On that arithmetic the investment looks clearly worthwhile. The mistake is to compare costs at an annual volume when the constraint binds monthly.

The lever is that the correct operations method is determined by the volume per production run, not by the annual average. The bench sells 48 000 units a year - 4 000 a month on average - but 80% of that volume is sold in three months, so the peak month requires 12 800 benches and the flow line can make 8 000. The shortfall of 4 800 a month must be produced in advance and stored. Storage of 14 400 benches at EUR 3 a bench a month for an average of four months costs EUR 172 800, which is nearly twice the EUR 96 000 saving the flow line creates. The method that is cheapest per unit is not the method that is cheapest to run.

The decision tree reinforces the conclusion and shows that it is robust. Flow is more expensive in both demand states, so the recommendation does not depend on the 0.6 probability. That is a stronger result than a single expected-value calculation would give, and it is worth saying so.

The second constraint - the twelve product variants - is there to show that the arithmetic is not the only obstacle. Flow production is only economic when a line can run without changeover, and Hartswood's range means eleven products would remain on batch. The investment would improve the cost of one product out of twelve while adding EUR 600 000 of fixed cost.

Classic wrong turns: comparing unit costs at the annual volume and ignoring capacity; dividing annual demand by twelve and using 4 000 as the monthly requirement; computing the decision tree without the storage cost; and concluding that flow must be better because 'higher volume means lower unit cost'.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 6.1 SWOT analysis and 6.3 STEEPLE analysis
questions.question:
The directors of Calderbank Print & Packaging must decide whether to spend EUR 60,000 on a faster leaflet press or to invest in packaging capability instead.

(a)

Explain how a SWOT analysis and a STEEPLE analysis differ in what they can tell the directors, using one example of each from the case.

[4]

(b)

Using the table, calculate each service line's share of total revenue in 2023 and in 2025, the change in total revenue over the period, and revenue per employee in each year. Comment on what the figures show.

[5]

(c)

Evaluate whether Calderbank should follow the SWOT and spend EUR 60,000 on the leaflet press, or act on the STEEPLE findings instead. Justify your answer.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) SWOT is an audit of the firm's own position. It sorts factors into strengths and weaknesses, which are internal and controllable, and opportunities and threats, which are external, and it is used to match the firm's resources to its environment. STEEPLE examines the external environment alone, across social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical factors, and is used to identify change that the firm does not control. (A1)(A1)

The difference matters here. The case example for SWOT is the supermarket leaflet contract, which the directors call a strength because it is long-standing and gives a predictable order book. The case example for STEEPLE is the social and technological shift away from printed leaflets towards supermarket apps, which is outside the firm's control and is shrinking the market for the product it prints. (A1)(A1)

(b) Total revenue: 2023 = 900 + 250 + 150 = EUR 1,300k; 2025 = 590 + 610 + 170 = EUR 1,370k. (M1)(A1)

Shares of total: leaflet printing falls from 900/1,300 = 69.2% to 590/1,370 = 43.1%; packaging rises from 250/1,300 = 19.2% to 610/1,370 = 44.5%; signage rises from 150/1,300 = 11.5% to 170/1,370 = 12.4%. (A1)

Total revenue rose by EUR 70k, or 5.4%, so the business looks as though it is growing. Revenue per employee: 2023 = 1,300,000/40 = EUR 32,500; 2025 = 1,370,000/40 = EUR 34,250. (M1)(A1)

The comment mark is for seeing that the headline is misleading. The total is up only because packaging has grown by 144%, from EUR 250k to EUR 610k, while the line the directors are defending has fallen by EUR 310k, or 34.4%, and is now smaller than packaging. The firm's future is already being decided by the line its SWOT calls a weakness. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The SWOT points one way. The leaflet contract is the firm's oldest relationship and its largest single order, and losing it would remove about 43% of revenue at a stroke. Spending EUR 60,000 on a faster press lowers the unit cost of the work the contract needs and may make Calderbank the cheapest bidder when the contract is next renewed. On this reading the EUR 60,000 protects the core of the business.

The STEEPLE reading contradicts it. The fall in leaflet revenue is not caused by anything inside the firm: readers are moving to apps, the supermarket has begun cutting print volumes, and the tax on virgin paper and extended producer responsibility raise the cost of the very product the press would print. A faster press makes Calderbank better at producing something its customer is buying less of. The weakness the SWOT admits, no packaging design experience, sits in the one line that is growing, and packaging faces rising demand because of the same environmental and legal pressures that are hurting leaflets. (A1)(A1)

A defensible answer can still support the press, because it buys time and cash while packaging capability is built. But the strongest answers notice that the two tools classify the same contract differently, as a strength internally and a threat externally, and recommend using the leaflet cash flow to fund packaging rather than to defend the declining line. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the two tools disagree about the same fact. The directors' SWOT is not careless: the supermarket contract really is the firm's largest and oldest relationship, and losing it would remove roughly 43% of revenue. Read internally, it is a strength and defending it is rational. Read through STEEPLE, the same contract is a threat, because the force reducing it - the shift to apps, the paper tax and extended producer responsibility - lies entirely outside the firm and cannot be managed by a better press.

The lever is that the obvious tool is the wrong one. A student who reaches for SWOT because the case is about the firm's position will produce a tidy four-box list and recommend the investment, but the analysis cannot show the trend, because a SWOT is a snapshot of factors, not a model of change. STEEPLE reveals the direction of travel, and the revenue table makes it quantitative: leaflets fall from 69.2% to 43.1% of revenue while packaging rises from 19.2% to 44.5%, so the firm's centre of gravity has already moved.

The trap is the total. Revenue rises by EUR 70k, or 5.4%, and revenue per employee rises from EUR 32,500 to EUR 34,250. A candidate who checks only these concludes that the business is healthy and the contract worth defending. The figure that contradicts this is the 34.4% fall in the leaflet line and the fact that it is now smaller than the packaging line the SWOT calls a weakness.

Classic wrong turns: treating the packaging weakness as a reason to stay with leaflets; listing STEEPLE factors without linking them to the falling line; and recommending diversification without noticing that the capability to diversify already exists inside the firm.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 6.2 Ansoff matrix and 6.4 Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix
questions.question:
The directors of Brackenwood Pet Foods must decide where to invest over the next three years.

(a)

Using the table, calculate the relative market share of each of the four products and classify each one using the BCG matrix. Show your working.

[5]

(b)

Explain how the Ansoff matrix would classify two growth options open to Brackenwood, using examples from the case.

[4]

(c)

Evaluate whether Brackenwood should follow the BCG recommendation to harvest Adult Complete. Justify your answer with reference to the Ansoff matrix and to the market data.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) Relative market share = own share divided by the largest rival's share. Puppy Complete 22/20 = 1.10; Adult Complete 34/18 = 1.89; Senior Care 7/26 = 0.27; Grain-Free Fresh 9/24 = 0.38. (M1)(A1)(A1)

Growth: Puppy Complete 14% (high), Adult Complete 3% (low), Senior Care 2% (low), Grain-Free Fresh 16% (high).

Classification: Puppy Complete is a star, with high growth and high relative share. Adult Complete is a cash cow, with low growth and high relative share. Senior Care is a dog, with low growth and low relative share. Grain-Free Fresh is a question mark, with high growth and low relative share. (A1)(A1)

(b) Ansoff classifies growth by whether the product and the market are existing or new. Market development means an existing product sold into a new market: Adult Complete sold through the supermarket value channel, which Brackenwood does not currently supply. The product already exists; only the market is new. (A1)(A1)

Market penetration means more of an existing product sold into the existing market: winning more shelf space for Adult Complete in the pet shops and garden centres it already uses. (A1)

Also creditable: product development, such as new Grain-Free recipes for existing premium customers, and diversification, a new product for a new market, which is the riskiest quadrant. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The BCG reading is clear. Adult Complete has a relative market share of 1.89 and market growth of only 3%, so it is a classic cash cow: the matrix says take its cash and invest it in the star, Puppy Complete. On the premium-segment numbers this is textbook, and harvesting means withdrawing promotion and product development from Adult Complete rather than reinvesting in it.

Ansoff contradicts that instruction. The lowest-risk growth available to Brackenwood is market development: taking the existing Adult Complete product into the supermarket value segment. That is a new market for an existing product, the second-least-risky quadrant, and it needs investment, which is exactly what harvesting removes. So the BCG instruction to take cash out of Adult Complete would close the one low-risk growth option the firm has.

The data make the clash worse. The classification depends on how the market is defined. Measured against the premium segment, Adult Complete has a relative share of 1.89; measured against the whole dog-food market, its share is 11% against the value leader's 13%, a relative share of 0.85, which is a dog, not a cash cow. The same product carries opposite BCG labels. The tool cannot settle the question until the directors decide which market they intend to compete in, and that is a strategic choice, not a calculation.

A defensible answer can still harvest: the firm is small, Puppy Complete is the star, and cash is scarce. The strongest answers notice that harvesting Adult Complete would destroy the Ansoff option the same product makes possible, and recommend funding market development of the cash cow instead. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that two accepted tools give opposite instructions about the same product. On the premium-segment data, Adult Complete is a textbook cash cow: 3% growth and a relative share of 1.89, five times the 0.38 of the question mark. The BCG logic is to take the cash it generates and put it into the star, Puppy Complete. A student who does the classification correctly and stops there will recommend harvesting.

Ansoff changes the answer, because it asks a different question. BCG asks where the cash is; Ansoff asks how risky growth would be. The least risky growth Brackenwood has is market development, the existing Adult Complete product sold into the supermarket value segment, which is precisely the product BCG has told the firm to stop investing in. Harvesting the cash cow and pursuing the Ansoff option are mutually exclusive, and the case does not say which the directors should prefer.

The lever is that the BCG classification is not a fact but a consequence of a choice about the market. Premium segment: relative share 1.89, cash cow. Whole market: 11% against 13%, relative share 0.85, dog. The matrix is often taught as though market share were given; here it is defined by the directors, and changing the definition changes the instruction. That is the point the strongest answers reach, and it is what makes the question a decision rather than an exercise in plotting.

Classic wrong turns: treating the BCG label as objective; recommending investment in the star without noticing that the firm has no cash because the cash cow is being harvested; placing market development in the diversification quadrant, which overstates its risk; and forgetting that the same product can be a cash cow and a dog at the same time.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 6.5 Business plan and 6.8 Circular business models
questions.question:
The founders of Dale & Vale Dairy must decide whether to commit to the returnable glass scheme in the business plan.

(a)

Explain two ways in which a circular business model such as returnable glass bottles could reduce Dale & Vale's costs, and one way in which it could increase them.

[4]

(b)

Using the figures, calculate the cost per delivery and the total annual cost of bottles and washing under plastic, under the plan's assumption of twenty uses, and under the trial's six uses. State the break-even number of uses and the payback period the plan implies.

[5]

(c)

Evaluate whether the business plan's proposal to switch to returnable glass bottles is sound. Justify your answer with reference to the trial, the bank's lending rule and the founders' objectives.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) A circular business model keeps materials in use rather than disposing of them after one cycle. Two ways it could cut Dale & Vale's costs. First, a glass bottle that is reused replaces many single-use bottles, so the dairy stops buying a new EUR 0.12 plastic bottle for every delivery. Second, it avoids the waste-disposal and packaging charges attached to single-use plastic and reduces exposure to future levies on single-use packaging. (A1)(A1)

One way it increases costs: the model needs reverse logistics. Bottles must be collected from households, returned to the depot, washed and refilled, which adds handling cost and requires the EUR 180,000 washer and store. The dairy also bears the cost of bottles that are broken or never returned. (A1)(A1)

(b) Annual deliveries = 3,000 households x 5 bottles x 52 weeks = 780,000 deliveries. (M1)(A1)

Plastic: cost per delivery EUR 0.12; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.12 = EUR 93,600. (A1)

Plan (20 uses): cost per delivery = 0.60/20 + 0.03 = EUR 0.03 + EUR 0.03 = EUR 0.06; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.06 = EUR 46,800. (M1)(A1)

Trial (6 uses): cost per delivery = 0.60/6 + 0.03 = EUR 0.10 + EUR 0.03 = EUR 0.13; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.13 = EUR 101,400. (A1)

Break-even uses: 0.60/u + 0.03 = 0.12 gives u = 0.60/0.09 = 6.67, so a glass bottle must be used at least seven times to be cheaper than plastic. (A1)

Payback on the plan's figures: annual saving = 93,600 - 46,800 = EUR 46,800; payback = 180,000/46,800 = 3.8 years. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The plan is internally consistent and looks attractive on its own assumptions. At twenty uses a bottle, glass costs EUR 0.06 a delivery against EUR 0.12 for plastic, a saving of EUR 46,800 a year, and the EUR 180,000 is repaid in 3.8 years, inside the bank's four-year rule. The bank's condition is therefore satisfied on the plan's numbers, and the circular model also delivers the founders' environmental objective.

The trial contradicts the assumption on which the whole plan rests. At six uses, glass costs EUR 0.13 a delivery, more than the plastic it replaces, and the annual cost rises to EUR 101,400, about EUR 7,800 a year worse than doing nothing. The break-even is seven uses, so the trial is not close: it falls below the point at which the investment stops destroying value. On the trial evidence the payback never arrives, and the bank's four-year rule is not met.

The evaluation therefore turns on a judgement about the trial. Ravi's argument has some force, because the trial lasted only three months and customers were told about the scheme a week before it began, so six uses may understate a mature scheme. Meg's argument is that the dairy cannot afford to be wrong, and the shortfall is a recurring EUR 7,800 a year, not a one-off. The strongest answers note that the plan should be rewritten with a range of reuse rates, that the scheme should be re-trialled with proper notice, and that the founders' zero-waste objective could be pursued at a smaller scale before EUR 180,000 is committed. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the business plan is arithmetically perfect and rests on a single assumption the case has already tested. On twenty uses a bottle, glass costs EUR 0.06 a delivery, saves EUR 46,800 a year and pays back the EUR 180,000 in 3.8 years, just inside the bank's four-year rule. Every figure the plan contains is correct. The mistake is not in the arithmetic but in the reuse rate, which the plan treats as a design choice and the trial reveals as an empirical result.

The lever is that the circular model inverts its own cost logic at a break-even the plan never states. Reuse replaces the repeated purchase of EUR 0.12 plastic bottles, but it adds reverse logistics: collection, washing and handling at EUR 0.03 a delivery, plus the capital cost of the washer. Break-even is 0.60/0.09 = 6.67 uses, so a bottle must survive seven trips before glass is cheaper. The trial managed six. Below that line, the more circular the model, the more it costs per delivery.

The clash of criteria is the second layer. The bank will lend only against a four-year payback, which the plan meets and the trial does not; the founders have a public zero-waste commitment, which the plan advances and the trial postpones. Neither objective can be satisfied at once on the evidence given, so the answer is a decision about which risk to accept, not a calculation. That is why the strongest answers propose rewriting the plan with a range of reuse rates and re-trialling with proper notice, rather than simply rejecting the scheme.

Classic wrong turns: accepting the plan's twenty uses; computing cost per delivery without the EUR 0.03 washing cost; treating the break-even as one use rather than seven; and concluding that the circular model must be cheaper because it is more sustainable.

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.5 Break-even analysis; 3.3 Costs and revenues
questions.question:
The proposed campaign would add €54 000 per year to fixed costs and is expected to change the sales mix to 60% supermarket / 40% online.

(a)

Calculate VF's weighted average contribution per unit at the current sales mix, and hence its break-even level of output.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the break-even level of output and the margin of safety at a volume of 620 000 units if the campaign achieves the expected 60 / 40 mix. Comment on why this result differs from the marketing director's claim.

[5]

(c)

Using the finance director's probabilities, calculate the expected annual profit both with and without the campaign. Evaluate, with reference to one stakeholder group and one non-financial factor, whether VF should launch the campaign.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) Contribution per unit = selling price − all variable costs.

Supermarket: $3.20-1.85-0.00=\textbf{€1.35}$ (A1)

Online: $5.00-1.85-1.10=\textbf{€2.05}$ (A1)

Weighted average contribution $=0.78(1.35)+0.22(2.05)=1.053+0.451=\textbf{€1.504 per unit}$ (M1)

$$\text{Break-even output}=\frac{\text{fixed costs}}{\text{contribution per unit}}=\frac{486\,000}{1.504}=323\,138\approx\textbf{323 000 units}$$ (A1)

(b) New weighted average contribution $=0.60(1.35)+0.40(2.05)=0.81+0.82=\textbf{€1.63 per unit}$ (M1)

New fixed costs $=486\,000+54\,000=\textbf{€540 000}$ (A1)

$$\text{New break-even output}=\frac{540\,000}{1.63}=331\,288\approx\textbf{331 000 units}$$ (A1)

$$\text{Margin of safety}=\frac{620\,000-331\,288}{620\,000}\times100=\textbf{46.6\%}$$ (A1)

The marketing director is right that contribution per unit rises, from €1.504 to €1.63. She is wrong that break-even falls: it rises, from about 323 000 to about 331 000 units, because fixed costs increase by 11.1% while weighted contribution increases by only 8.4%. The margin of safety also falls, from 47.9% to 46.6%. (A1)

(c) Profit = (volume × weighted contribution) − fixed costs.

*Without the campaign (contribution €1.504, fixed €486 000):*

  • at 620 000 units: $620\,000(1.504)-486\,000=932\,480-486\,000=\textbf{€446 480}$
  • at 480 000 units: $480\,000(1.504)-486\,000=721\,920-486\,000=\textbf{€235 920}$

$$\text{EV}=0.6(446\,480)+0.4(235\,920)=267\,888+94\,368=\textbf{€362 256}$$ (M1)(A1)

*With the campaign (contribution €1.63, fixed €540 000):*

  • at 620 000 units: $620\,000(1.63)-540\,000=1\,010\,600-540\,000=\textbf{€470 600}$
  • at 480 000 units: $480\,000(1.63)-540\,000=782\,400-540\,000=\textbf{€242 400}$

$$\text{EV}=0.6(470\,600)+0.4(242\,400)=282\,360+96\,960=\textbf{€379 320}$$ (M1)(A1)

The campaign has the higher expected profit by €17 064, about 4.7% of the expected profit without it. (A1)

*Evaluation.* On expected value the campaign is justified, and it is more robust than the margin of safety suggests: because the campaign is better in both states of the world (€470 600 > €446 480, and €242 400 > €235 920), the decision does not actually depend on which probability is correct. The break-even volume *of the change itself* is $54\,000\div(1.63-1.504)=428\,571$ units, and both volume scenarios exceed it. (A1)

However the expected-value calculation hides a step change rather than a smooth one. Supermarket buyers are the stakeholder group at risk: they supply 60% of volume even after the shift, and their reaction to a supplier promoting direct-to-consumer sales is not a 40%-chance event — it is a decision they either make or do not. If delisting removed the supermarket channel entirely, the 480 000-unit scenario would be optimistic. Set against that, a non-financial factor pulls the other way: chilled single-household delivery carries a markedly higher carbon footprint per unit than palletised supermarket distribution, which sits awkwardly with the sustainability positioning of a plant-based brand and could damage the very customers the campaign targets.

Conclusion (AO3): a supported recommendation. The expected gain of €17 064 is thin relative to a channel-specific risk that the model does not capture, so a full campaign is hard to justify on these numbers; the stronger recommendation is to test the online offer in a limited region, or to grow online volume without advertising it to supermarket customers, so that the contribution gain is captured without triggering the delisting risk. (A1)
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a trap that is invisible until the arithmetic is done. Almost every student — and, in the scenario, the marketing director — reasons that a higher contribution per unit must lower break-even. It does not, because the campaign buys that higher contribution with €54 000 of extra fixed costs, and break-even is a ratio of the two. Break-even rises and the margin of safety falls, which looks like a clear argument against the campaign.

The twist is that break-even is the wrong decision criterion here. VF sells 620 000 units against a break-even of about 330 000, so it operates far above the break-even point; in that region what matters is total contribution, not the level at which profit becomes zero. Expected profit is higher with the campaign in *both* volume states, which means the conclusion is insensitive to the probability estimates — a much stronger argument than the €17 064 figure alone suggests.

The evaluation mark separates description from judgement. Naming 'supermarket buyers' as a stakeholder earns nothing; observing that their response is a step change the probability model cannot represent does. And the sustainability point is not decoration: chilled home delivery is genuinely more carbon-intensive per unit than palletised freight, so the campaign works against the positioning of the product it is promoting.

The indifference volume makes the robustness claim exact, and it is worth stating. Because the same contribution and fixed costs apply in both volume states, the campaign's advantage does not depend on the probabilities at all: it is the better choice at any volume above the point where $1.63V - 540\,000 = 1.504V - 486\,000$, that is $V = 54\,000 / 0.126 = 428\,571$ units. Both states lie above that threshold, so the recommendation is robust - but the low state of 480 000 units sits only about 12% clear of it, which is why the answer is a qualified yes rather than a comfortable one.
